stem: Which one of the following genetic abnormalities would you expect in this case?
options: Retinoic acid receptor, alpha (RARα) gene mutation
explanation:
C-myc proto-oncogene translocation
The likely diagnosis in this case is Burkitt's lymphoma. This is a B-cell lymphoma that is historically classified in three different forms: endemic, sporadic and immune-deficiency associated. The endemic form is prevalent where malaria is endemic, including equatorial Africa and certain areas in Brazil. Though the pathophysiology of this fast-growing lymphoma is not completely understood, Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) infection is known to play a major role. EBV can escape T-cell meadiated immune response and it then remains latent in B-lymphocytes in the germinal centre at the level of the lymph nodes. This may lead to cell immortalisation and excessive proliferation. Malaria is thought to aid this process by inhibition of EBV-specific immune response. One of the most characteristic genetic features in Burkitt lymphoma is the classic t(8;14) reciprocal translocation, resulting in the transposition of the c-myc proto-oncogene with one of the immunoglobulin heavy chain genes, leading to dysregulated cell proliferation. This genetic abnormality is present in up to 85% of all cases. Burkitt's lymphoma presents in different ways according to each different form. In the endemic disease, jaw and facial bone involvement is more frequent and associated with non-tender neck lymphadenopathy. In the sporadic form, abdominal involvement is more prevalent, so that patients often present abdominal distension, ascites or bowel obstruction. Immunodeficiency-related Burkitt's lymphoma usually presents with predominant lymph node involvement. The microscopic appearance is typically described as 'starry sky', due to scattered macrophages phagocytising cell debris and apoptotic cells. However, such pattern can be seen in other types of high-grade lymphomas.

Philadelphia chromosome
Philadelphia chromosome is the resulting product of the translocation between chromosome 9 and 22. The juxtaposition of the locum BCR and ABL creates a hybrid gene, that leads to the production of an abnormal tyrosine-kinase (BCR-ABL1), which is constantly active and promotes uncontrolled cell proliferation. This genetic feature is found most often in chronic myeloid leukaemia.

RET proto-oncogene mutation
RET proto-oncogene codes for a tyrosine-kinase and can be subjected to a variety of different somatic rearrangements, germ-line or more frequently point mutations. This may result in abnormal signalling towards uncontrolled cell proliferation. RET mutations are well described in the pathogenesis of papillary carcinoma and MEN2 syndrome.

Retinoic acid receptor, alpha (RARα) gene mutation
The RARA gene codes for a transcription factor called RARα. This protein is important in the maturation of myeloid cells beyond the stage of promyelocytes. In acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML) a translocation between chromosome 15 and 17 creates the fusion gene PML-RARα. The resulting protein binds DNA, represses gene transcription, effectively blocking myeloid differentiation at the level of promyelocyte. The disrupted activity of PML gene also promotes abnormal proliferation.

Breast cancer (BRCA) gene mutation
BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumour suppressor genes involved in the pathogenesis of breast and ovarian cancer. Different types of mutations of these genes are found in the hereditary breast-ovarian cancer syndrome. In addition, BRCA mutations have been linked to increased risk of other cancers, such as colon, pancreatic and prostatic cancer. Both BRCA genes produce proteins that are involved in the repair of double-stranded DNA breaks. A disruption in such enzymatic pathway leads defective DNA repair and potential cancerous transformation.

stem: A 49-year-old woman undergoes a mastectomy for an invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. The doctors in the unit where she is managed are interested in utilising tumour markers to monitor for possible recurrence of her disease, in addition to radiological and clinical surveillance. Which one of the following markers has potential utility in monitoring breast cancer?
explanation:
CA 15-3
CA 15-3 is a tumour marker associated with breast cancer and as such can be used as a general indicator of tumour burden and possible metastasis, although it is not specific to neoplastic disease and may show low level elevations in benign breast disease or hepatic cirrhosis. Additionally, small elevations in CA 15-3 may be seen in hepatic or pancreatic cancers. CA15-3 is not sufficiently sensitive to be used as a diagnostic marker for breast cancer, as up to 30% of tumours will not be associated with a rise in the marker.

Acid phosphatase
Acid phosphatase is incorrect. Acid phosphatase was used historically to monitor prostatic carcinoma before the advent of PSA measurement.

CA 19-9
CA 19-9 is incorrect. CA 19-9 is a tumour marker used in the monitoring of pancreatic cancer.

CA 125
CA 125 is incorrect. CA 125 is an ovarian tumour marker.

HCG
HCG is incorrect. HCG may be a useful marker in monitoring germ-cell tumours.

stem: An elderly patient presents with a 4-month history of night sweats, weight loss, low appetite and change in bowel habits. A CT abdomen pelvis shows a large mass with contrast enhancement in the transverse colon. The patient's bloods are analysed, and negative acute phase proteins are reduced. Which one of the following is a negative acute phase protein?
explanation:
Albumin
Albumin, together with other proteins such as transferrin, transthyretin, retinol-binding protein and antithrombin, decreases during inflammation. A possible theory behind this process proposes that amino acids are redirected to produce positive acute phase proteins, which are increased in inflammatory processes.

Interleukin (IL) 6
This is a positive acute phase protein, which means it is increased during an inflammatory status.

Tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-alpha
TNF-alpha is a positive acute phase protein; therefore, it is increased during an inflammatory status.

Transforming growth factor (TGF)-beta
TGF-beta is an immune-regulatory cytokine, which may be increased in cancer and certain autoimmune disease.

Rheumatoid factor (RF).

stem: A 55-year-old solicitor with known stomach cancer is admitted with intractable nausea and vomiting. He tells you he is participating in a phase II trial for a new chemotherapeutic agent. What is the purpose of such a trial?
options: To compare a new drug with the best conventional therapy
To determine the long-term toxicity of a drug
To establish the anti-tumour activity of a drug
To establish the human toxicity of a drug
To study the pharmacokinetics of a drug
explanation:
To establish the anti-tumour activity of a drug
Phase II trials are used to establish the anti-tumour activity of a drug. At the same time, further information on optimal dosing and common adverse effects may be gained.

To compare a new drug with the best conventional therapy
To compare a new drug with the best conventional therapy is incorrect. Phase III trials compare a new drug with the best conventional therapy and usually require large numbers of consenting patients.

To determine the long-term toxicity of a drug
To determine the long-term toxicity of a drug is incorrect. Phase IV studies are used to determine the long-term toxicity of a drug.

To establish the human toxicity of a drug
To establish the human toxicity of a drug is incorrect. Phase I trials are used to establish the human toxicity of a drug by delivering carefully selected increased doses to fit patients.

To study the pharmacokinetics of a drug.

stem: What are the tumour cells called that are found in patients with Hodgkin’s disease?
explanation:
Reed–Sternberg cells
Reed–Sternberg cellsare the name for the tumour cells that are found in Hodgkin’s disease. The cells are named after Dorothy Reed and Carl Sternberg, who provided the first definitive microscopic description of Hodgkin’s disease. These are specific types of giant cells that are found in the lymph node biopsies of patients with Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Philadelphia cells
Philadelphia cells is incorrect. There is no such cell; the Philadelphia chromosome is found in CML.

Cytotoxic lymphocytes
Cytotoxic lymphocytes is incorrect.

Activated lymphocytes
Activated lymphocytes is incorrect.

Langerhans’ cells
Langerhans’cells is incorrect. These are dendritic cells of the skin and mucosa. Hodgkin’s.

stem: A 64-year-old male heavy smoker is admitted to hospital with haemoptysis. Routine laboratory tests reveal a blood calcium level of 3.21 mmol/l (2.2–2.6). Which one of the following is the probable underlying cause of his presentation?
explanation:
Squamous-cell lung cancer
Squamous-cell lung carcinomas make up around 25–30% of all lung cancers and are associated with PTHrp production, causing hypercalcaemia. Squamous-cell lung cancer also commonly metastasises to bone (as does thyroid, breast and prostate cancer and lymphomas), which may cause hypercalcaemia.

Large-cell lung cancer
Large-cell lung cancer is incorrect. Large-cell lung cancer comprises a group of subtypes of tumour, the most significant of which is large-cell neuroendocrine tumours. These may cause hypercalcaemia but are significantly rarer than squamous-cell lung cancer.

Sarcoid
Sarcoid is incorrect. Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous disease which is associated with hypercalcaemia but is usually diagnosed between 20 and 40 years of age and is not smoking related, therefore less likely in this scenario.

Small-cell lung cancer
Small-cell lung cancer is incorrect. Small-cell lung cancer may also metastasise to bone causing hypercalcaemia, but it is a rarer feature than in squamous-cell lung cancer.

stem: A 75-year-old man has been recently started on all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA), which is the mainstay of treatment in the presence of retinoic-acid receptor alfa (RARα) mutations. Which of the following conditions is associated with this genetic abnormality?
explanation:
Acute pro-myelocytic leukaemia
Acute pro-myelocytic leukaemia (APML) is a subtype of acute myeloid leukaemia characterised by a chromosomal translocation involving the RARα on chromosome 17. The most common translocation occurs between the promyelocytic leukaemia gene on chromosome 15 (approximately 90% of the cases). The resulting fusion gene produces altered proteins, which interfere with the production of granulocytes. RARα mutations can be overcome by all-trans retinoic acid, which is the mainstay of treatment, though not all mutations are sensitive, in which case the prognosis is poorer.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma
RET mutations are well described in the pathogenesis of papillary carcinoma. RET proto-oncogene codes for a tyrosine-kinase and can be subjected to a variety of different somatic rearrangements, germ-line or more frequently point mutations. This may result in abnormal signalling towards uncontrolled cell proliferation.

Medullary thyroid carcinoma
RET proto-oncogene is recognised in the pathogenesis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2), an inherited cancer syndrome characterised by the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and parathyroid hyperplasia. MEN2 is further divided into three subtypes: MEN2A, MEN2B and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma (FMTC), depending on the organs involved.

Pheochromocytoma
Pheochromocytoma has been described as part of the MEN2 syndrome, which is a familial condition that predisposes to different cancers, including medullary thyroid carcinoma and parathyroid hyperplasia. RET proto-oncogene mutations are a well-described feature in the pathogenesis of MEN2.

Parathyroid hyperplasia
RET mutations are associated to an inherited cancer syndrome, MEN2. Though there are various subtypes, parathyroid hyperplasia is certainly one of the described features.

stem: A 56-year-old Asian woman presents with weight loss, lethargy and night sweats. Her investigations show progressive kidney disease and 2.1 g/day of proteinuria. A renal biopsy shows glomerular and vascular deposition of a pink amorphous material, which shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining. The deposits are positive for lambda light chains. Which one of the following diseases is she most likely to have?
explanation:
Multiple myeloma
This patient has multiple myeloma with renal amyloidosis. Amyloid is classified chemically according to the type of fibril protein: the most common forms encountered clinically are the AL and AA types. Lambda light chains are specific to the AL type of amyloid protein, which occurs in multiple myeloma and monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS), formerly considered as ‘primary amyloid’ conditions. Primary amyloidosis is more common in men over 50 years (2 : 1), and the prognosis is poor. Chemotherapy such as melphalan and prednisolone (± autologous stem cell transplant) may be required. In the elderly or frail, an alternative treatment is pulsed dexamethasone, alkylating agents and interferon.

Rheumatoid arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis forms 40% of secondary amyloid.

Tuberculosis
Tuberculosis is a rare cause of renal amyloid and, as a secondary amyloid, is therefore an incorrect option in this case. Furthermore, there would be other symptoms such as fever and respiratory symptoms.

Systemic lupus erythematosus
Systemic lupus erythematosus is not usually associated with renal amyloidosis. Other types of fibril protein are associated with hereditary renal amyloidosis and central nervous system (CNS) amyloid.

Secondary amyloidosis
Secondary amyloidosis involves serum amyloid A proteins which are an acute-phase reactant in patients with chronic inflammation. The prognosis depends on the cause of the inflammation.

stem: A 54-year-old male presents to his GP with jaundice and is found to have a painless enlargement of the gallbladder (Courvoisier’s law). Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater
explanation:
Carcinoma of the ampulla of Vater
Courvoisier’s law: If the malignant obstruction is below the level of the cystic duct, the gallbladder is distended and may be palpable. The urine is dark and the stools pale; a film of blood on the pale stool may give it a silvery colour (‘silver stools’). An ultrasound or CT scan examination will reveal dilatation of the biliary tree and may demonstrate the level of the obstruction. Ultrasound-guided percutaneous needle biopsy may be employed to provide a histological diagnosis. Bile duct carcinoma frequently causes obstruction at the porta hepatis and, consequently, at laparotomy the extrahepatic biliary tract appears non-dilated. Even if an operative cholangiography is performed, the contrast medium frequently fails to pass the obstruction and fill the dilated intrahepatic biliary tree. It is important to establish the diagnosis precisely before surgery is contemplated by performing an ERCP (endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography) or PTC (percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography). This is particularly important because most of these patients are best treated by endoscopic or percutaneous biliary stents rather than by surgery.

Carcinoma of the gallbladder
Carcinoma of the gallbladder is incorrect. Gallbladder carcinoma is usually painful, but may cause similar symptoms (jaundice, enlarged gallbladder) so it may be impossible to distinguish clinically from ampullary carcinoma.

Gallstones in the cystic duct
Gallstones in the cystic duct is incorrect. Gallstones are painful and typically cause symptoms after ingesting a fatty meal.

Liver cirrhosis
Liver cirrhosis is incorrect. Liver cirrhosis may cause jaundice and if acute may cause some hepatomegaly, but in the chronic condition is associated with a shrunken nodular liver.

Progressive hepatitis B.

stem: A 26-year-old man is admitted with a 1-week history of worsening headaches and visual disturbance. Some 6 months ago he completed a course of intensive chemotherapy for widespread advanced testicular cancer. On examination there are visual field abnormalities and papilloedema. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his symptoms and signs?
explanation:
Relapse with brain metastases
The symptoms and signs are indicative of raised intracranial pressure; given the original advanced nature of the disease, a relapse with brain secondaries seems most likely. If the diagnosis is confirmed on imaging, urgent treatment with steroids should be commenced in order to reduce intracranial pressure, followed by appropriate definitive management (second-line cytotoxic chemotherapy).

Cerebral abscess
Cerebral abscess is incorrect. A cerebral abscess would be less likely given the timescale, but is an important differential diagnosis.

Late chemotherapy toxicity
Late chemotherapy toxicity is incorrect. Late chemotherapy neurotoxicity usually manifests as a peripheral neuropathy (with the exception of ototoxicity).

Paraneoplastic phenomenon
Paraneoplastic phenomenon is incorrect. Neurological paraneoplastic syndromes typically present with encephalitis, cerebellar dysfunction or brainstem dysfunction.

Side-effect of cranial irradiation
Side-effect of cranial irradiation is incorrect. Cranial irradiation may cause lethargy, alopecia and some longterm cognitive impairment.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with breast cancer underwent a left modified radical mastectomy for an intraductal carcinoma 2 years ago. She now presents to the Emergency Department with confusion, lethargy and thigh pain. X-ray reveals a sclerotic lesion in the shaft of a femur. Which one of the following is the most likely blood abnormality?
explanation:
Calcium increased
Malignancy is the most common cause of hypercalcaemia in hospital patients, and breast and lung cancers are the most frequently associated with this condition. Hypercalcaemia of malignancy is caused by either osteolytic bony metastases with local release of cytokines, or by tumour secretion of parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) and/or 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol). Clinical manifestations of hypercalcemia involve the gastrointestinal tract(nausea, vomiting, constipation), central nervous system (weakness, lethargy, confusion, coma) and kidneys (polyuria, thirst).

Calcium decreased
Calcium decreased is incorrect. Bone metastasis would be very unlikely to cause hypocalcaemia.

Glucose increased
Glucose increased is incorrect. Symptoms of lethargy and confusion may be associated with severe hyperglycaemia (eg in hyperosmolar non-ketotic state), but this is not suggested by the scenario and there is no mention of the patient being diabetic.

Potassium decreased
Potassium decreased is incorrect. As described above, alterations in potassium status are important in cancer patients who are undergoing chemotherapy and are at risk of tumour lysis syndrome and kidney disease, but are not directly related to the diagnosis of skeletal metastasis.

Potassium increased.

stem: A 26-year-old woman complains of irregular menstrual periods, milky discharge from the breast and fatigue. She is found to have prolactin levels of 100 ng/ml (normal value 0–25 ng/ml). A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is performed, which confirms the presence of a 9-mm pituitary lesion, with no mass effect or chiasm compression. What is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Start cabergoline
Prolactinomas are benign tumours that arise from the pituitary gland and constitute around 40% of all pituitary neoplasms. Prolactinomas are classified as micro-prolactinomas if < 10 mm and macro-prolactinomas if > 10 mm. Though they can present at any age, they are more frequent in women. The clinical presentation may include lethargy, malaise, irregular or absent periods, galactorrhoea, excessive hair growth, dyspareunia and, with larger tumours, headache, visual problems or neurological deficit. The pituitary growth can impair the production of other important hormones, such as thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) and adreno-corticotropic hormone (ACTH). It is therefore important to measure pituitary hormones levels if there is suspicion of a neoplastic growth. Medical treatment is preferred to surgery, which is reserved for refractory cases or in the instance of significant mass effect, chiasm compression or neurological deficit. First-line treatment includes cabergoline or bromocriptine, with the former being preferred in view of fewer side-effects and higher response rate in clinical trials. Cabergoline is an ergot derivate, with a stimulant effect on dopamine receptors in the brain, resulting in the inhibition of prolactin release.

Endoscopic trans-sphenoidal surgical resection
The likely diagnosis in this scenario is prolactinoma, a benign tumour of the pituitary gland, which most commonly presents in women. Over the last two decades, surgery has become less used, in favour of medical treatment with dopamine agonists, such as cabergoline or bromocriptine. As there are no adverse features in this scenario, the best treatment option is to start cabergoline.

Radiotherapy
The underlying diagnosis in this case is a pituitary prolactinoma, which appears to be small (< 10 mm), with no mass effect, chiasm compression or neurological deficits. Therefore, first-line treatment should include a dopamine agonist, such as cabergoline, with the aim of inhibiting prolactin release from lactotrophic cells. Radiotherapy is reserved for refractory cases, where both surgery and medicines have failed. With radiotherapy, prolactin levels may decrease very slowly, hence patients often remain on dopamine agonists during the treatment.

Chemotherapy
Prolactinomas are non-cancerous tumours of the pituitary. Chemotherapy does not have a role in the treatment of the disease, which is usually addressed with dopamine agonists or, in more difficult cases, surgery/radiotherapy.

Transcranial surgery
Surgery has certainly a role in the treatment of prolactinomas, especially when they are above 10 mm of diameter or medical treatment has failed. Transcranial surgery is more invasive and nowadays less preferred compared to trans-sphenoidal resection. In this scenario, the most appropriate first-line treatment is to start cabergoline, a dopamine agonist, with the aim of reducing prolactin release.

stem: A 39-year-old man undergoes treatment for a high tumour burden, non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma with a regimen that includes cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine and prednisolone. The treatment is complicated by E. coli bacteraemia, for which he is admitted to hospital and given gentamicin and ceftazidime. Twenty-four hours after admission he is oligoanuric (urine output 250 ml in 24 hours), his blood pressure is 150/60 mmHg and he has peripheral oedema. Urinalysis shows a pH of 5.5 and +1 protein, and urine microscopy reveals numerous reddish-brown, rosette-like crystals. His plasma creatinine concentration is 200 μmol/l, calcium is 1.76 mmol/l and phosphate is 2.72 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the oliguria?
explanation:
Tumour lysis syndrome
Tumour lysis syndrome typically occurs after chemotherapy for lymphoma with a large tumour burden. Virtually all affected patients are oligoanuric, with an acidic urine containing numerous uric acid crystals and calcium phosphate precipitation and crystal formation. Now that allopurinol prophylaxis is frequently employed in highrisk patients, the incidence has declined. However, it does still occur and is now more often due to the severe hyperphosphataemia and occasionally xanthinuria (as allopurinol inhibits the metabolism of xanthine to uric acid), rather than hyperuricaemia. Hyperkalaemia is also seen, due to acute cell lysis. A phosphate level above 2.5 mmol/l (resulting in hypocalcaemia due to calcium phosphate precipitation) and hyperuricaemia support the diagnosis.

Ceftazidime-induced interstitial nephritis
Ceftazidime-induced interstitial nephritis is incorrect. Interstital nephritis secondary to cephalosporin therapy is uncommon, and frequently associated with dipstick haematuria. It would not be expected to present with such profound oligoanuria, nor proteinuria or crystals.

Gentamicin nephrotoxicity
Gentamicin nephrotoxicity is incorrect. Gentamicin nephrotoxicity usually results in non-oliguric kidney disease. Therefore, it would not be expected to present with such profound oligoanuria, nor proteinuria or crystals.

Lymphomatous infiltration of the kidney
Lymphomatous infiltration of the kidney is incorrect. Lymphomatous renal infiltrate may present acutely with oligoanuria by way of obstructive uropathy; this is a very rare presentation in lymphoma.

Vincristine nephropathy.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with fatigue, night sweats and unintentional weight loss over the past six months. On examination, he has palpable cervical lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly. Blood tests reveal a white blood cell count of 30 x 10 9/L with an increased lymphocyte count. Which of the following is the best diagnostic test to confirm this condition?
options: CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
explanation:
Flow cytometry
Flow cytometry is considered the best diagnostic test for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL). This technique allows for detailed analysis of cell surface markers on leukocytes, which can identify clonal B-cell populations characteristic of CLL. It provides rapid results and is less invasive compared to other options, such as bone marrow biopsy or surgical procedures. Moreover, flow cytometry not only confirms the diagnosis but also helps in staging and prognostication by identifying specific immunophenotypic patterns.

Bone marrow biopsy
Although bone marrow biopsy can provide definitive histological confirmation of CLL by revealing infiltration with small mature-appearing lymphocytes, it is not typically required for diagnosis in all cases of CLL due to its invasive nature. Flow cytometry on peripheral blood is usually sufficient for establishing a diagnosis without subjecting patients to unnecessary procedures.

CT scan of the chest, abdomen and pelvis
CT scans are useful in assessing disease extent in terms of organ involvement, such as enlarged nodes or splenomegaly. However, they do not provide definitive cellular characteristics needed for diagnosing CLL. Imaging studies are more often used later in disease management rather than at initial diagnosis.

Lymph node excisional biopsy
While an excisional lymph node biopsy could reveal histopathologic features consistent with CLL/small lymphocytic lymphoma (SLL), it involves a surgical procedure that may be unnecessary given that flow cytometry can diagnose CLL using peripheral blood samples non-invasively. It could be considered in case of suspicion of transformation to a high-grade lymphoma.

Peripheral blood smear.

stem: A 35-year-old man has been recently diagnosed with chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML). He would like to know what the possible treatments are for his condition. Which of these drugs acts against the abnormal BCR-ABL tyrosine kinase signalling, which is typically detected in patients with CML?
explanation:
Imatinib
Imatinib is a tyrosine-kinase inhibitor (TKI) directed against BCR-ABL tyrosine-kinase. This kinase is the product of an abnormal fusion gene, which is formed by reciprocal translocation between chromosome 9 and 22, t(9;22) (q34;q11). This is called Philadelphia chromosome, which is abnormally short and contains the fusion gene BCR-ABL1, created by the juxtaposition of the BCR gene (breakpoint cluster region) and the proto-oncogene ABL1. The resulting gene codes for a tyrosine kinase, which is constantly activated, driving uncontrolled cell division. Philadelphia chromosome is not only found in CML but can also be observed in acute lymphoblastic leukaemia and occasionally in acute myeloid leukaemia. Since the introduction of Imatinib, several other TKIs have been produced: ponatinib, dasatinib, nilotinib and bosutinib are all used in the treatment of CML.

Rituximab
Rituximab is a monoclonal antibody directed against CD20 protein, which is expressed on B-lymphocytes. Rituximab is widely used in CLL, certain types of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma and in non-malignant illnesses (eg autoimmune haemolytic anaemia).

Bortezomib
Bortezomib is a proteasome inhibitor, which controls protein expression and function, participating in the degradation of ubiquitylated or misfolded proteins. Its main indication is in the treatment of multiple myeloma.

Ixazomib
Ixazomib is a proteasome inhibitor used in the treatment of myeloma. Proteasomes control protein expression and function, having a role in degradation of ubiquitylated or misfolded proteins.

stem: What is the first-line intervention of choice for controlling her symptoms?
explanation:
Octreotide
Octreotide is a long-acting somatostatin analogue which blocks release of 5-HT, and probably also reduces tissue sensitivity to 5-HT in target tissues. For patients with unresectable carcinoid, the diagnosis here, it is the intervention of choice for symptom relief.

Conventional chemotherapy
Conventional chemotherapy is incorrect. Mid-gut carcinoid tumours (the likely primary source here) are poorly responsive to conventional chemotherapy, although new regimens including combination therapy with capecitabine and temozolamide are useful in some patients.

Cyproheptadine
Cyproheptadine is incorrect. Other hormone antagonists including cyproheptadine, clonidine and methysergide may be useful in patients who fail to respond to octreotide alone.

Interferon-α
Interferon-α is incorrect. Interferon-α is effective at controlling symptoms (and may have an antitumour effect) in some patients; this is thought to be due to modulation of the host immune response to the carcinoid tumours.

Methysergide
Methysergide is incorrect. Although restricted for use in other conditions such as migraine because of risk of retroperitoneal fibrosis, use of methysergide can be useful in metastatic carcinoid where symptoms are resistant to octreotide alone.

stem: A 60-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents with fever. She received palliative treatment with paclitaxel chemotherapy 10 days ago. She now complains of a painful vesicular rash along her right thorax. Physical examination shows an acutely ill-looking woman. Her oral examination, as well as chest, cardiac and abdominal examination, is normal. There is a vesicular erythematous rash on her chest. Her temperature is 39°C. Laboratory examination is normal except for a haemoglobin of 10.5 g/litre, WCC 1.1 × 10 9/litre and platelets 30 × 10 9/litre. Chest X-ray is normal. Blood cultures are obtained. Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation:
Parenteral aciclovir and ceftazidime
This lady is acutely unwell with a rash on her chest that suggests herpes zoster. She is leukopenic and thrombocytopenic, and febrile. She therefore needs broad spectrum antibiotics, as well as aciclovir to treat the presumed herpes zoster.

Granulocyte colony-stimulating factor (G-CSF)
G-CSF is incorrect. G-CSF might be required to shorten the duration of neutropenia, but the most appropriate step in this lady’s management is broad spectrum antibiotics to treat neutropenic sepsis.

Platelet infusion
Platelet infusion is incorrect. Platelet infusion is not required here. British guidelines suggest infusing platelets in the presence of sepsis if the platelet count is less than 20.

Tamoxifen
Tamoxifen in incorrect. Tamoxifen is not appropriate. This lady needs treating for sepsis.

Second course of paclitaxel
A second course of paclitaxel is incorrect. A second course of paclitaxel is not the most appropriate next step for similar reasons.

stem: A patient presents with jaundice. Physical examination reveals an enlarged, nodular liver. CT scan of the abdomen shows a cirrhotic liver with a large mass, and the CT-guided biopsy of the mass demonstrates a malignant tumour derived from hepatic parenchymal cells. Infection with which one of the following viruses would most likely be directly related to the development of this tumour?
explanation:
Hepatitis B virus
Quantitatively, chronic infection with hepatitis B virus is one of the most significant causes of cancer in many parts of the world. In China, for example, liver cancer accounts for about 20% of all cancer deaths, the large majority of which are a result of chronic lifelong infection with the virus. Infant vaccination against the virus is now being introduced and will protect the new generation, but will not provide retrospective protection.

Epstein–Barr virus
Epstein–Barr virus is incorrect. Epstein–Barr virus is associated with the development of Burkitt’s and Hodgkin’s lymphomas and some central nervous system malignancies.

Human herpes virus 8
Human herpes virus 8 is incorrect. Human herpes virus 8 is associated with the development of Kaposi’s sarcoma in immunosuppressed patients.

Human papillomavirus
Human papillomavirus is incorrect. Human papillomavirus (in particular type 16 and 18) is associated with the development of cervical, anal and oro-pharyngeal cancers.

Human T-lymphocyte virus
Human T-lymphocyte virus is incorrect. Human T-lymphocyte virus is associated with the development of leukaemia.

stem: A 58-year-old businessman presents with bilateral leg weakness that has suddenly become worse over the last 12 hours. Some 10 months ago he had a lobar resection for a stage-II squamous-cell carcinoma followed by radiotherapy and adjuvant chemotherapy. He has had a dull ache in his lower back over the past 3 months, but put this down to arthritis from when he used to play rugby as a young man. On examination there is reduced power and altered sensation in both legs. Which one of the following is the most likely cause of the current problem?
options: Spinal cord compression as a result of vertebral metastases
explanation:
Spinal cord compression as a result of vertebral metastases
Spinal cord compression as a result of vertebral metastases is the correct answer here. This man has bilateral leg weakness which has come on suddenly, with a background history of lung cancer. He has both reduced power and altered sensation in both legs. This is therefore spinal cord compression until proved otherwise. The most common cancers to give rise to spinal cord compression are breast, bronchus, prostate, multiple myeloma and high-grade non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma. Urgent MRI scanning should be performed.

Paraneoplastic myelopathy
Paraneoplastic myelopathy is incorrect. The patient has evidence of neurological involvement, with reduced power and altered sensation.

Peripheral neuropathy secondary to carcinomatosis
Peripheral neuropathy secondary to carcinoma is incorrect. This comes on slowly, but the clinical history here is a sudden onset of bilateral leg weakness.

Secondary spinal tumour deposit
Secondary spinal tumour deposit is incorrect. Secondary spinal tumour deposit is possible, but this does not necessarily impinge on the spinal cord, whereas this man clearly has evidence of neurological involvement.

Spinal tuberculosis
Spinal tuberculosis is incorrect. Spinal tuberculosis is very rare. There is nothing in the history to suggest this.

stem: A 21-year-old man is referred by his General Practitioner due to a 3-month history of progressive and worsening shortness of breath on exertion, associated with lethargy, weight loss and night sweats. He has no past medical history and takes no medications; he smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks alcohol each weekend. Chest and cardiac examination are unremarkable, although there is a palpable 3-cm neck lymph node which is firm and non-tender to touch. A chest X-ray reveals an enlarged mediastinum, but no significant lung abnormalities. Which of the following investigations is likely to be the most useful in reaching a diagnosis?
options: Fine-needle aspiration of neck lymph node
Excisional biopsy of neck lymph node
explanation:
Excisional biopsy of neck lymph node
The case described suggests an underlying diagnosis of lymphoma in view of the typical age group, symptoms and evidence of neck/mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Pathological diagnosis should be made from an excisional lymph node biopsy or a sufficiently large surgical specimen. Subsequent staging and risk stratification are carried out through CT neck–chest–abdomen–pelvis, PET scan, full blood count, blood chemistry, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and viral screening.

Fine-needle aspiration of neck lymph node
The most likely underlying diagnosis in this scenario is lymphoma. A fine-needle aspiration may miss the histological diagnosis as it allows only a small portion of the lymph node to be examined. The best option to achieve a histological diagnosis is to perform an excisional lymph node biopsy.

Computed tomography (CT) chest–abdomen–pelvis
The age of the patient, together with his symptoms and chest X-ray findings, suggest a diagnosis of lymphoma. Though a CT chest–abdomen–pelvis is certainly useful and part of the staging process, it will not provide a histological diagnosis and will not guide targeted treatment.

Positron-emission tomography (PET)
The main suspicion in this scenario is that the patient has lymphoma. PET scan is an important part of the staging process; however, it cannot provide and histological diagnosis, which is best sought through a lymph node biopsy.

Full blood count.

stem: A 69-year-old man who is treated with imatinib for a gastrointestinal stromal (GIST) tumour comes to the oncology clinic for review. Which of the following correctly represents the mode of action of imatinib in GIST?
explanation:
Kit inhibitor
Imatinib inhibits several receptor tyrosine kinases, but it is inhibition of the product of c-kit that makes it of value in the treatment of GIST. Kit is the receptor for stem cell factor, which is thought to be a driver for the development of GIST. Other receptor tyrosine kinases inhibited by imatinib include: Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase (TK), the discoidin domain receptors (DDR1 and DDR2), the colony stimulating factor receptor (CSF-1R) and the platelet-derived growth factor receptors alpha and beta (PDGFR-alpha and PDGFR-beta); however, these options are incorrect because they are not the driver mutations most commonly present in GIST.

Bcr-Abl inhibitor
Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase (TK) is incorrect. Bcr-Abl tyrosine kinase (TK) is another receptor tyrosine kinase inhibited by imatinib. However, this option is incorrect because it is not the driver mutation most commonly present in GIST.

B-Raf inhibitor
B-Raf is incorrect. B-Raf inhibitor is an oncogene known to be important in the development of several tumours, and two B-Raf inhibitors have recently been licensed for the treatment of malignant melanoma (e.g. vemurafenib).

DDR-1 inhibitor
DDR-1 inhibitor is incorrect. The discoidin domain receptors (DDR1 and DDR2) are other receptor tyrosine kinases inhibited by imatinib. However, this option is incorrect because it is not the driver mutation most commonly present in GIST.

PDGFR-alpha inhibitor
PDGFR-alpha inhibitor is incorrect. The platelet-derived growth factor receptors alpha and beta (PDGFR-alpha and PDGFR-beta) are other receptor tyrosine kinases inhibited by imatinib. However, this option is incorrect because it is not the driver mutation most commonly present in GIST.

stem: A 61-year-old woman comes for review in the Outpatient Clinic. She has a longstanding history of chronic gastritis, for which she has been taking omeprazole regularly for several years. During the past six months, she has complained of persistent sense of fullness and nausea, especially after meals. As a consequence, she has lost a significant amount of weight. To further investigate these symptoms, she underwent a computed tomography (CT) chest–abdomen–pelvis, which reports a diffuse, severe and homogeneous thickening of the gastric wall (20 mm), with peri gastric lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue (MALT) lymphoma
The longstanding history of gastritis, coupled with rapid loss of weight and worsening sense of fullness and nausea, suggest a possible underlying upper gastro-intestinal tract malignancy. The CT findings are typical of MALToma. Though there are other possible differentials, such as diffuse gastric carcinoma (linitis plastica), sarcoidosis and Crohn’s disease, MALT lymphoma appears the most likely in view of the age group and the long history of chronic gastritis. This also raises the suspicion of H. pylori chronic infection, which is a well-described risk factor for developing gastric malignancies, especially MALTomas. The MALT is a collection of lymphoid cells within the mucosa of different organs, in particular gastrointestinal, respiratory and genitourinary tract. MALT is normally involved in antigen recognition and immune response at the level of the mucosa. MALT lymphomas are considered extra-nodal manifestations of marginal-zones B-cell lymphomas. In the majority of cases, they are low-grade tumours, however, a minority may present or evolve towards more aggressive forms.

Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) infection
Though H. pylori infection may be suspected due to the longstanding history of chronic gastritis and the symptoms described, the rapid loss of weight, coupled with the CT findings is in keeping with a gastric malignancy, most likely a MALToma. H. pylori infection is recognised as risk factor for the development of MALT lymphomas, which occurs in the stomach most frequently. In more than 90% of patients, MALT lymphomas are associated with H. pylori infection.

Atrophic gastritis
Atrophic gastritis may result from chronic inflammation, which may have different causes, with autoimmune disorders and chronic H.pylori infection being the most common. In atrophic gastritis, the normal gastric epithelium is replaced by fibrous and intestinal tissue, resulting into abnormal secretion of hydrochloric acid, pepsin and intrinsic factor among others. In this scenario, though the patient is known to have chronic gastritis, the CT appearance, coupled with the rapid clinical deterioration, suggest underlying malignancy.

Crohn’s disease
Crohn’s disease is an inflammatory bowel disease with a multi-factorial and complex aetiology, that is characterised by chronic gut inflammation, potentially affecting any part of the gastrointestinal tract. Patients tend to be diagnosed years after symptoms onset. Although Crohn's can occur at any age, diagnosis usually occurs between 15–35 years of age. In this scenario, the symptoms of chronic gastritis, without any vomiting or diarrhoea, with a recent deterioration and loss of weight, do not fit with Crohn's. Moreover, in gastric Crohn's, inflammatory changes may be noticed on CT; however, it would be homogeneous, as in this case.

Gastric ulcer disease
Gastric ulcers disrupt the architecture of the gastric epithelium, resulting in fibrosis and intestinal transformation. They would not cause a homogeneous thickening, especially if above 10 mm of width, as in this case. The CT findings and the clinical scenario are in more in keeping with a MALT lymphoma. Non-Hodgkin’s.

stem: A 78-year-old man is being treated for pancreatic cancer with chemotherapy and radiotherapy. At his clinic appointment, he complains of intermittent shooting pain starting from the epigastrium and radiating across the abdomen, which he has tried to control with paracetamol and codeine, but with no improvement. He reports no issues with bowels opening, no vomiting and no pyrexia. An abdominal examination is unremarkable with a soft, non-tender abdomen. A computed tomography (CT) abdomen and pelvis shows no acute abdominal pathology. What is the next most appropriate symptomatic treatment?
options: Stop codeine and start regular oral morphine
explanation:
Add gabapentin
This patient has pancreatic cancer and reports intermittent shooting pains around epigastrium and radiating across the abdomen. In absence of obvious acute abdominal pathology on examination and imaging, neuropathic pain from coeliac plexus compression is suspected. Neuropathic pain can be addressed with adding ‘adjuvant medications’, which include gabapentin, pregabalin, duloxetine or amitriptyline. Refractory pain should be referred to pain specialists to consider further intervention such as coeliac plexus block.

Stop codeine and start regular oral morphine
The most likely issue in this case is coeliac plexus compression, especially with normal abdominal examination and CT imaging. Oral morphine alone would not address neuropathic pain and adjuvant medications should be considered, such as gabapentin, amitriptyline, pregabalin or duloxetine.

Add ibuprofen
Because coeliac plexus compression from pancreatic cancer is the suspected underlying diagnosis here, ibuprofen will not help in controlling neuropathic pain; therefore, other adjustments would need to be made to the analgesic plan for this patient.

Add lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is a sodium-channel inhibitor, whose main indication is in the treatment of epilepsy. In the context of neuropathic pain, lamotrigine can be considered; however, it should not be prescribed outside the specialist setting and it is not first-line treatment.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with weight loss, fatigue and malaise. He has a background of Child’s Pugh B cirrhosis secondary to alcoholic liver disease. He has been abstinent from alcohol for three years, and currently takes 200 mg spironolactone per day. He has previously required large volume paracentesis to assist with fluid removal. On examination, his abdomen is soft with a positive shifting dullness test suggestive of a mild to moderate amount of ascites. His alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is 400 ng/ml and a carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) is 2.4 ng/ml. A computed tomography (CT) thorax, abdomen and pelvis demonstrates a single 3.5-cm liver lesion, with no other lesions noted. There is no evidence of invasion into the portal venous system or other vascular invasion. What is the optimal management option for this patient?
options: Folinic acid, fluorouracil and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) chemotherapy
explanation:
Liver transplant
Given the liver lesion on CT, raised AFP and background of cirrhosis, this man likely has hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). There is no evidence of metastasis or vascular invasion. As he meets the Milan criteria (which can be used to assess suitability for liver transplant in patients with HCC) which includes tumour size ≤ 5 cm or up to three tumours ≤ 3 cm, and no extrahepatic or major vessel involvement, liver transplant may be a potential option for him.

Folinic acid, fluorouracil and oxaliplatin (FOLFOX) chemotherapy
FOLFOX chemotherapy is a combination chemotherapy regimen usually used in the treatment of colorectal carcinoma, so would not be suitable in this case.

Radiofrequency ablation
A liver transplant would offer a better chance of survival compared to radiofrequency ablation and systemic sorafenib immunotherapy.

Sorafenib immunotherapy
Liver transplantation would offer a better chance of survival for this patient in comparison to systemic sorafenib immunotherapy.

Surgical resection of lesion.

stem: A 68-year-old with known small-cell lung carcinoma presents with a history of increasing confusion and seizures over a period of several weeks. There are no focal neurological signs and haematological and biochemical investigations are normal. A brain CT and MRI are normal. What underlying cause do you suspect?
explanation:
Paraneoplastic disorder
Paraneoplastic neurological disorders (PNDs) are rare syndromes that are caused by, or associated with, an underlying malignancy. PNDs do not occur by direct tumour involvement in neural tissue, but are thought to be caused by crossed antigenicity or tumour-peptide release. PNDs can affect many parts of the nervous system and, unlike most gradual neurodegenerative disorders, PNDs typically exhibit a rapid onset of symptoms. Although PNDs most often occur in small-cell lung cancer, they can also be caused by a variety of other cancers including breast, colon and testicular cancers. Neurological PNDs include encephalitis, myelopathy, neuropathy, myopathy, cerebellar degeneration and the Eaton–Lambert syndrome (myasthenic syndrome, resulting from an inappropriate immune response to the neuromuscular junction). Other types of PND include endocrine (eg Cushing syndrome, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion); mucocutaneous (eg dermatomyositis, acanthosis nigracans) and haematological (eg polycythaemia), as well as pyrexia of unknown origin.

Alzheimer’s dementia
Alzheimer’s dementia is incorrect. The timescale is too short for Alzheimer’s dementia.

Cerebral metastases
Cerebral metastases is incorrect. The normal CT/MRI makes cerebral metastases unlikely.

Septicaemia
Septicaemia is incorrect. Sepsis is an important differential diagnosis and needs to be excluded.

Steroid related
Steroid related is incorrect. Steroids in high doses can cause a psychosis but are unlikely to cause seizures given the normal biochemistry.

stem: A 39-year-old, previously well, woman is referred to you with a 3-month history of asthma and wheezing with occasional episodes of haemoptysis. She also tells you that she might be perimenopausal as she has had severe episodes of flushing. You suspect there might be an underlying pathological process. Which one of the following investigations is most likely to reveal a cause?
explanation:
Urine 5-hydroxyindolacetic acid
Levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA), a breakdown product of serotonin metabolism, are raised in carcinoid syndrome. This syndrome is characterised by tachycardia, flushing, bronchoconstriction, haemodynamic instability and diarrhoea, and occurs in up to 10% of patients with bronchial carcinoid tumours.Some 25% of patients with a carcinoid pulmonary tumour are asymptomatic; however, the majority of symptomatic patients have symptoms directly involving the bronchopulmonary tree, such as persistent atelectasis, recurrent pneumonia, pulmonary abscess and bronchiectasis. Carcinoid syndrome occurs in up to 10% of cases of pulmonary carcinoid tumours, much less frequently than in cases associated with gastrointestinal carcinoid tumours. Bronchopulmonary carcinoid tumours are reported to represent about 10% of all carcinoid tumours and 1–5% of all lung tumours are carcinoid tumours.

Urine calcium
Urine calcium is incorrect. Urine calcium levels will be increased if there is hypercalcaemia, for example as a complication of squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung; this would be associated with abdominal pains, constipation, nausea and vomiting.

Urine catecholamines
Urine catecholamines is incorrect. Urine catecholamines are increased in phaeochromocytomas, which would be associated with hypertension, tachycardia and headaches.

Urine cortisol
Urine cortisol is incorrect. Increased urine levels of cortisol may indicate an ACTH-secreting tumour, which would cause Cushingoid symptoms (weight gain, hirsutism, skin thinning, osteoporosis).Bronchial carcinoid tumours may produce ACTH, as may adrenal adenomas, medullary thyroid tumours and pancreatic islet cell tumours.

Urine vanillylmandelic acid
Urine vanillylmandelic acid is incorrect. Urine vanillylmandelic acid levels are increased in phaeochromocytomas which would be associated with hypertension, tachycardia and headaches.

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with postmenopausal bleeding. She has no significant past medical history and is otherwise in good health. An ultrasound reveals a thickened endometrial lining. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Endometrial cancer
Postmenopausal bleeding is a red flag symptom of endometrial cancer, especially in women over the age of 60. The finding of a thickened endometrium on ultrasound further raises suspicion as it can indicate malignant changes within the uterine lining. Early detection allows for better prognosis and management outcomes. Given her age and presentation, endometrial cancer remains the most plausible diagnosis.

Endometrial hyperplasia
While this condition can also present with postmenopausal bleeding and an increased thickness of the endometrium, it typically occurs due to unopposed oestrogen stimulation without subsequent progesterone exposure, which may not be relevant here given her lack of hormone therapy history or other risk factors presented.

Endometrial polyp
Polyps are benign growths that can cause abnormal uterine bleeding. However, they are less common causes compared to malignancies in postmenopausal women presenting with these symptoms. Additionally, polyps usually do not cause significant thickening of the entire endometrium, as seen on ultrasound.

Hormone replacement therapy-induced bleeding
Breakthrough bleeding or spotting would be an important consideration due to the hormonal changes if the patient was on hormone replacement therapy (HRT), especially during the initial stages of HRT or when the dosage is adjusted. However, there is no mention of such treatment in her medical history provided here. Furthermore, HRT-related bleeds typically do not result in generalised thickening seen in imaging studies like ultrasounds.

Uterine fibroid
Fibroids are benign smooth muscle tumours that are commonly present during reproductive years and might lead to heavy menstrual periods but are less likely to manifest as new-onset postmenopausal bleeding combined with diffuse thickening of the endometrium at this patient's age.

stem: Which of the following tests would be most expected to be abnormal?
explanation:
Calcium levels
The presence of anaemia, thrombocytopenia, increased IgG and a monoclonal band on serum protein electrophoresis suggests a diagnosis of multiple myeloma. In such context, the symptoms described in this scenario (confusion, nausea and distended abdomen suggesting constipation) would raise the suspicion of hypercalcaemia, therefore, this is the most likely option in this case. Hypercalcaemia in multiple myeloma has multifactorial aetiology; however, a major contributor is widespread tumour-induced bone destruction. This is enhanced due to increased osteoclastic activity, resulting in bone reabsorption, caused by specific cytokines locally expressed/released by the myeloma cells.

Lymphocyte count
The symptoms at presentation and the blood results raise the suspicion of underlying multiple myeloma. Lymphocytes count might be decreased in these cases; however, it is often normal. Considering the presence of abdominal distension, nausea and confusion, hypercalcaemia would most be expected to be abnormal.

International normalised ratio (INR)
The INR is a derived measure of prothrombin time (PT), introduced in order to overcome the variability in results among laboratories with different types of analytical systems. Therefore, the INR/PT is an assay evaluating the extrinsic and common pathway in the coagulation cascade in the setting of warfarin prescription. In the case described, there is concern for underlying multiple myeloma, which is often associated with hypercalcaemia.

Computed tomography (CT) head
CT head may be part of the confusion screening in a patient presenting with unexplained impaired cognitive function. In this scenario, the presence of paraprotein and raised IgG suggests a diagnosis of myeloma. Therefore, the clinical scenario of confusion, abdominal pain and nausea would make more likely to detect hypercalcaemia.

Thyroid function tests
Thyroid function tests are certainly part of the confusion screening in a patient with unexplained impaired cognitive function. Hypothyroidism can cause constipation and confusion, especially in the elderly and most severe cases. However, in this scenario, the most likely underlying diagnosis is myeloma, therefore, calcium levels would be most expected to be abnormal and would also fit the described clinical scenario.

stem: Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation to help establish the likely underlying primary diagnosis?
options: Serum protein electrophoresis, urine protein electrophoresis and serum-free light chain
explanation:
Serum protein electrophoresis, urine protein electrophoresis and serum-free light chain
This woman has suspected multiple myeloma as evidenced by anaemia, thrombocytopenia, raised calcium, IgG levels, deranged renal function, longstanding back pain and probable pathological vertebral fracture. Multiple myeloma is a progressive malignant disease of the plasma cells that normally produce immunoglobulins. The condition is characterised by a proliferation of abnormal monoclonal immunoglobulins in the blood, referred to as paraproteinaemia. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, in the first instance, serum protein electrophoresis and serum-free light chain assay should be used to confirm the presence of a paraprotein indicating possible myeloma or monoclonal gammopathy of unknown significance (MGUS). In the presence of an abnormal serum electrophoresis, serum immunofixation can confirm the paraproteinaemia. However, serum protein electrophoresis, serum immunofixation, serum free light chain assay or urine electrophoresis (urine Bence–Jones protein assessment) alone cannot exclude a diagnosis of myeloma: a bone marrow biopsy should be performed to confirm the presence of monoclonal plasma cells. In addition, other secondary care investigations include whole body MRI or CT, where MRI is not available or possible. Skeletal survey is now considered obsolete; however, it can be performed if both CT and MRI are not feasible. In addition, X-rays of symptomatic areas for people with bone pain should also be performed, to rule out pathological fractures. Tertiary care tests may be performed, such as fluorescence in situ hybridisation analysis of bone marrow aspirate, serum beta 2 microglobulin concentration and next-generation DNA sequencing (if locally available).

Bone marrow aspirate and trephine
A bone marrow aspirate and trephine should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of multiple myeloma and assess prognostic features via flow cytometry and immunophenotyping.

Whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)/computed tomography (CT)
Whole-body MRI/CT is part of the staging process and should be offered to all patients with a new diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

Peripheral blood film
Performing a peripheral blood sample is useful to look for rouleaux (aggregations of red blood cells), which might suggest underlying paraproteinaemia and can be considered as an additional investigation, but it is not the next most useful in the diagnostic process.

stem: A 45-year-old woman undergoing her third cycle of intensive chemotherapy for breast cancer is admitted via the medical take. She has been suffering from a sore throat for some 12–16 h and has now begun a fever with profuse sweating. On admission to the Emergency Department she has a pyrexia of 38.2°C. She has an indwelling, tunnelled, subcutaneous catheter for chemotherapy. Which one of the following micro-organisms is most likely to be responsible for her fever?
explanation:
Staphylococcus epidermidis
Summarising febrile neutropenia aetiology: Commonly, febrile neutropenia is said to be due to Gram-positive organisms such as Staphylococcus epidermidis or Streptococcus viridans (around 60% of cases). Around 30% of cases may be due to Gram-negative bacteria such as E. coli, Klebsiella spp. or Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Other organisms, such as candida, corynebacterium, cytomegalovirus (CMV) or varicella zoster virus, make up the other 10% of cases. A microbiological diagnosis, however, is only made in around 40% of cases. Source of infection: Indwelling intravenous catheters are often the cause of Staph. epidermidis infection. Infection with viridans streptococci may be related to mucositis or previous quinolone treatment. It is important to take multiple samples of blood from indwelling lines and peripheral sites for culture, and to culture urine and faeces, arrange viral serology and to send the tips of any lines for culture. Treatment: Antibiotic therapy should be started before the results of the cultures are available, but, if possible, not before samples are taken. The standard regime recommended by NICE is piperacillin and tazobactam. Platelet counts may fall rapidly in response to sepsis, and platelet transfusion may be necessary in some cases.

Candida albicans
Candida albicans is incorrect. Candida can cause varied problems, from local membrane infections to widespread dissemination. It is a commensal organism of the skin but can become pathogenic and cause localised infection, normally secondary to change in the host flora. Invasive focal infection can occur through haematogenous spread, with anatomical abnormalities or devices providing entrance into the host, and this is more likely in neutropenic or ITU patients in whom visceral dissemination can occur. However, the symptoms suggest neither a localised infection nor infection of her PICC line site, making Candida albicans unlikely.

Acinetobacter sp
Acinetobacter sp., is incorrect. This is a common Gram-negative coccobacillus associated with hospital, especially ITU, admission. It is isolated commonly in ventilator-associated pneumonia, central line infections and catheter-associated UTIs. In the absence recent of hospital admission or ITU stay, this is less likely.

Escherichia coli
Escherichia coli is incorrect. E. coli is a common Gram-negative organism which is associated with enteric and urinary infections. Infection would be associated with either gastrointestinal, biliary or urinary symptoms, and the absence of such symptoms makes infection with this organism less likely.

Klebsiella sp
Klebsiella sp. is incorrect. This is a Gram-negative bacillus which causes urinary and respiratory tract infections. It most commonly causes infections in people with compromised immunity and is a common nosocomial agent and would be far more likely with biliary symptoms or recent hospital admission.

stem: What is the next most appropriate intervention?
options: Arrange transfer to the Emergency Department to receive appropriate treatment
Collect blood cultures and give intravenous (IV) antibiotics
explanation:
Collect blood cultures and give intravenous (IV) antibiotics
The recent chemotherapy, presence of low-grade fever, hypotension and tachycardia triggers concern for neutropenic sepsis. In such context, IV antibiotics administration must not be delayed, as there is a significant increase in mortality with delaying treatment above one hour from presentation. Patients on chemotherapy and especially those with neutropenia, cannot mount an efficient immune response and can deteriorate rather rapidly. The United Kingdom ‘Sepsis Six’ bundle delineates the fundamental steps to be considered in approaching septic patients: give O 2 if SaO 2 is less than 94% on room air take blood tests and microbiology samples give IV broad-spectrum antibiotics give IV fluids to restore tissue perfusion check serial lactates measurements check urine output and monitor fluid balance.

Arrange transfer to the Emergency Department to receive appropriate treatment
Arranging transfer to a different department may be appropriate in order to offer the patient a setting that suits their clinical needs. However, this should not delay essential management, especially with suspected neutropenic sepsis. Hence, the next most appropriate action should be to collect microbiology samples and administer IV antibiotics.

Give IV 5% dextrose
The patient described in this scenario has most likely developed a urinary tract infection and she also shows signs of sepsis (hypotension, tachycardia, low-grade pyrexia). Because she has received chemotherapy only two weeks prior to presentation, there is a high chance this may be a case of neutropenic sepsis. Giving IV antibiotics would therefore carry priority in the described scenario. IV fluid administration is certainly part of sepsis management; however, this would in the form of normal saline or Hartmann’s solution.

Catheterisation to monitor urine output
The scenario presents a patient with signs and symptoms of sepsis, possibly triggered by a urinary tract infection. Though it is important to monitor urine output and fluid balance, catheterisation would not be the next best step in this scenario. When suspecting neutropenic sepsis, it is vital not to delay administration of IV antibiotics, preceded, when possible, by blood sample collection, including microbiology tests.

Give oral antibiotics
The patient has received chemotherapy two weeks prior to presentation and she is therefore at risk of neutropenia. Tachycardia, hypotension and low-grade pyrexia are all red flags for sepsis and should be considered seriously in cancer patients, whose impaired immune system cannot provide an appropriate response to infection. In view of this, IV antibiotics should be promptly administered and patient should be admitted to hospital for further sepsis management.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely cause of the rapid deterioration seen here?
explanation:
Haemorrhage into a metastasis
The rapid deterioration, seen over the course of a few hours, is most suggestive of haemorrhage into a metastasis. Teratomas are well known to metastasise via haematogenous spread, including to liver, lung, bone and brain.

Cerebral infarction
Cerebral infarction is incorrect. Given the high likelihood of a cerebral metastasis, there is no reason to expect an alternative, additional diagnosis such as infarction.

Cerebral oedema
Cerebral oedema is incorrect. A slow build-up in symptoms is usually due to cerebral oedema, which is progressive, surrounding the metastasis.

Rapid growth of a metastasis
Rapid growth of a metastasis is incorrect. Rapid growth of a metastasis is unlikely given the time frame of hours, even for very aggressive malignancy.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Given the high likelihood of a cerebral metastasis, there is no reason to expect an alternative, additional diagnosis such as subarachnoid haemorrhage.

stem: A 65-year-old smoker presents with progressive left shoulder pain of several weeks duration. On direct questioning he admits to a reduction in power and sensation affecting his left hand. Shortly after his initial presentation he develops visual disturbances and a left-sided ptosis. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vertebral disc prolapse of the cervical spine
explanation:
Pancoast tumour
A tumour in the superior pulmonary sulcus (Pancoast tumour) can cause progressive constant pain in the shoulder, upper anterior chest or interscapular region, soon spreading to the arm once the brachial plexus is invaded. Other symptoms of this type of tumour include weakness and atrophy of the muscles of the hand, Horner syndrome (visual disturbance and ptosis), hoarseness and spinal cord compression at levels T1 and T2.

Carpal tunnel syndrome
Carpal tunnel syndrome is incorrect. Carpal tunnel syndrome causes symptoms in the hand and wrist.

Coronary heart disease
Coronary heart disease is incorrect. Coronary heart disease is associated with exertional left-sided chest pain.

Syringomyelia
Syringomyelia is incorrect. Syringomyelia is a rare condition in which an irregular fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) causes a central cord syndrome, usually affecting the cervical area, but may extend the whole length of the cord. Typically, in early adult life the patient notices weakness and wasting of an upper limb and/or loss of the sensation of pain. There is usually areflexia in the arms, a spastic paraparesis and a dissociated sensory loss (retention of common touch and proprioception sense with loss of pain and temperature sensation) in the upper limbs.

Vertebral disc prolapse of the cervical spine
Vertebral disc prolapse of the cervical spine is incorrect. A prolapsed vertebral disc in the cervical spine would cause pain in the neck and shoulder radiating into the arm, and if severe may be associated with loss of power and sensation in the upper limbs, but would not cause visual symptoms or ptosis.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner complaining of fatigue and intermittent headaches. He has no known past medical history of note. He consumes one bottle of wine per week and smokes 15–20 cigarettes/day. On examination, he is cachectic and appears fatigued. He is afebrile, and has a heart rate of 80 bpm and a blood pressure of 124/66 mmHg. There is no focal neurology on examination. Haemoglobin is 108 g/l (normal value 115–155 g/l) and sodium is 120 mmol/l (normal value 135–145 mmol/l). Which of the following is the most appropriate investigation to help confirm the underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Chest X-ray
This patient has a history of smoking, with lethargy, anaemia and cachexia. Small cell lung cancer is associated with paraneoplastic syndromes such as syndrome of inappropriate anti-diuretic hormone through ectopic antidiuretic hormone production. Of the options given in this question, a chest X-ray is the only investigation that will aid in the diagnosis of lung cancer.

Early morning cortisol
A morning cortisol reading is useful in the investigation of hyponatraemia, with a low result indicating hypoadrenalism as an underlying cause. Hypoadrenalism is unlikely in this patient.

Plasma and urinary osmolalities
Paired osmolalities are useful in the investigation of hyponatraemia. The history of smoking, combined with anaemia and cachexia, makes lung malignancy a likely cause of the patient’s hyponatraemia, for which a chest X-ray is the most appropriate diagnostic test.

Plasma protein and lipid levels
Plasma protein and lipid levels are checked in patients with hyponatraemia, as their derangement can cause pseudohyponatraemia. Although it is important to have these levels checked, it is unlikely to be diagnostic, given this patient’s presentation.

Urinary sodium
Urinary sodium will help to ascertain if the cause of hyponatraemia is due to renal salt wasting or extrarenal losses. It would not, however, be diagnostic for this patient.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with irregular vaginal bleeding, especially postcoital and pelvic pain. On examination, the cervix appears friable with contact bleeding with erosions. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Cervical cancer
Cervical cancer is characterised by symptoms such as irregular vaginal bleeding, particularly post-coital bleeding, and pelvic pain. A friable cervix with erosions that bleeds on contact is a classic sign of cervical malignancy. High-risk human papillomavirus (HPV) infection is a significant risk factor for developing cervical cancer. Timely recognition and referral for colposcopy and biopsy are crucial for early diagnosis and management.

Endometrial cancer
Endometrial cancer typically presents with abnormal uterine bleeding but more commonly affects postmenopausal women rather than younger women like this patient. It usually involves heavy menstrual periods or intermenstrual spotting rather than just post-coital or irregular patterns of bleeding seen in cervical pathology. The presence of a friable cervix and erosions on examination points away from endometrial involvement as it suggests localised cervical changes rather than endometrial origin.

Cervical ectropion
Cervical ectropion is a benign condition and can cause postcoital bleeding due to exposure of the columnar epithelium of the endocervix to the vaginal milieu but typically present with excessive vaginal discharge. Furthermore, the appearance may be similar; however, it lacks other concerning signs like friability erosions and associated with malignancy, which makes cervical ectropion less likely in this context.

Pelvic inflammatory disease
Pelvic inflammatory disease often presents with lower abdominal pain, fever, and purulent discharge alongside pelvic discomfort but does not generally cause a visibly friable cervix and erosions upon examination without other significant findings such as adnexal tenderness or systemic symptoms like fever, which are absent here.

Uterine fibroids
Uterine fibroids can lead to abnormal uterine bleeding. However, they do not typically cause a friable cervix and erosions nor would they explain the specific symptom of post-coital spotting described here without additional mass effect symptoms like bulk-related pressure effects or palpable abdominal masses indicative of fibroid presence.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely to be raised?
explanation:
Cancer antigen–19–9
Cancer antigen–19–9 is particularly raised in pancreatic cancer, although it may be raised in other gastrointestinal neoplasms (including gastric) and benign pancreatic pathology. Given this patient’s history, including classical features such as jaundice and an epigastric mass, the most likely primary source is a pancreatic tumour.

Alpha fetoprotein
Alpha-fetoprotein is associated with hepatocellular (liver) carcinoma. Although this malignancy can cause similar symptoms, including jaundice and upper abdominal pain, a palpable and painless mass in the epigastrium is more likely to be pancreatic cancer.

Carcinoembryonic antigen
Carcinoembryonic antigen is associated with gastrointestinal cancers, including colon and gastric cancer. It would not be significantly elevated in a patient with pancreatic cancer.

Cancer antigen–125
Cancer antigen–125 is unlikely to be raised in this man, as it is a tumour marker for ovarian cancer.

Prostate-specific antigen
Prostate-specific antigen is associated with prostatic carcinoma. Although it is a more common malignancy in men, it would not cause jaundice which suggests a hepatobiliary or pancreatic malignancy.

stem: A 58-year-old Chinese man visiting relatives in the UK presents with a 3-month history of weight loss, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain. On examination there is hepatomegaly. Both transaminases and alkaline phosphatase are elevated. He does not smoke and drinks alcohol only occasionally. Which type of malignancy is most likely to account for this presentation?
explanation:
Hepatocellular carcinoma
Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common primary hepatic tumour and one of the most common cancers worldwide. HCC is rare in the western hemisphere where the most common causes of HCC are alcoholic cirrhosis, anabolic steroid use and haemochromatosis. HCC is more common in Asia and Africa where the common causes of HCC are hepatitis B, hepatitis C and aflatoxin exposure. Liver function tests can be normal, and α-fetoprotein (AFP) levels may be raised because this protein is commonly produced by HCC; however, over one-third of patients have normal AFP levels. The other cancers listed (ie pancreatic carcinoma, cholangiocarcinoma, stomach cancer and oesophageal cancer) could all present in a similar manner by metastasising to the liver.

Cholangiocarcinoma
Cholangiocarcinoma is incorrect. Cholangiocarcinoma could present in a similar manner but it is a less likely cause than HCC.

Oesophageal cancer
Oesophageal cancer is incorrect. Oesophageal cancer could present in a similar manner but HCC is a more likely cause for the presentation described.

Pancreatic carcinoma
Pancreatic carcinoma is incorrect. Although pancreatic carcinoma could present in a similar manner, it is less likely here than HCC.

Stomach cancer
Stomach cancer is incorrect. Although stomach cancer could present in a similar manner, HCC is a more likely cause of the presentation described.

stem: A 65-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with worsening back pain over the past two months. He has a history of prostate cancer diagnosed three years ago, treated with radical prostatectomy and androgen deprivation therapy. On examination, there is tenderness over the lumbar spine but no neurological deficits. What is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the most likely cause of his symptoms?
options: Plain radiography of the lumbar spine
explanation:
Bone scintigraphy
Bone scintigraphy (bone scan) is highly sensitive for detecting bone metastases, which are common in patients with a history of prostate cancer presenting with new-onset back pain. It can identify areas of increased osteoblastic activity indicative of metastatic disease even before structural changes become apparent on other imaging modalities like X-rays or CT scans.

CT scan of the abdomen
While a CT scan can provide detailed images and help assess abdominal organs for metastatic disease, it does not specifically target bone metastases as effectively as a bone scintigraphy does. In this case, since his primary complaint is back pain and he has tenderness over his lumbar spine, an imaging modality focused on bones would be more appropriate.

MRI of the lumbar spine
Although MRI provides excellent soft tissue contrast and detailed imaging useful for assessing spinal cord compression or nerve root involvement from tumours or metastasis, it should be a whole-body MRI not only of the lumber spines to screen the whole body for marrow abnormalities to be comparable with the advantage of radionuclide bone scanning in imaging of the whole skeleton.

Plain radiography of the lumbar spine
Plain radiographs are less sensitive than bone scans in detecting early metastatic lesions; they often miss small or subtle lytic/sclerotic changes associated with bony metastasis until they are quite advanced. Radiographs might show structural damage once significant destruction has occurred but aren't reliable for initial detection.

Serum alkaline phosphatase levels
Although elevated serum alkaline phosphatase can indicate increased osteoblastic activity consistent with bony metastasis from cancers like prostate cancer, it lacks specificity and sensitivity compared to imaging studies such as bone scans, which directly visualise skeletal involvement.

stem: What is the most likely underlying cause of these findings?
explanation:
Lung cancer
The signs and symptoms described suggest the presence of superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO). The underlaying conditions can be malignant or non-malignant, the latter being much less common nowadays. Patients can present with dyspnoea, facial swelling, ‘head fullness’, cough, dysphagia. These symptoms are exacerbated by bending forward or lying down. Typical signs include facial swelling, distended neck and chest wall veins, upper limbs oedema, facial plethora, cyanosis, cognitive dysfunction or coma. Among malignant causes, lung cancer accounts for up to 70% of the cases, followed by non-Hodgkin lymphoma at approximately 10%. Rarer causes of SVCO (less than 10%) include breast cancer, thymic and mediastinal germ cell tumours. Nowadays, non-malignant aetiologies are much rarer than in the past. These include infections (eg syphilis, tuberculosis, histoplasmosis, actinomycosis), ascending aortic aneurysm, mediastinal fibrosis, vasculitis and artero-venous fistula. In this scenario, the long smoking history, hypercalcaemia and chest examination, with right upper zone dullness/reduced entry and neck lymphadenopathies, make lung cancer the most likely underlying aetiology.
