Once SVCO is diagnosed, there are three main treatment options: surgical management, radiotherapy or stenting. The management decision is taken upon the type of cancer, stage and performance status. If the primary malignancy is unknown, it is important to obtain a tissue diagnosis before starting treatment.

Syphilis
The case describes a classic presentation of SVCO. Syphilitic aortic aneurysm can be responsible for SVCO; however, this patient has a long smoking history, non-tender and firm neck lymphadenopathies and hypercalcaemia, suggesting malignancy is the most likely aetiology.

Tuberculosis (TB)
TB with extensive mediastinal nodes involvement is a rare cause of SVCO. This patient has several red flags suggesting underlying malignancy; therefore, tuberculosis is not the most likely option.

Non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is certainly one of the possible causes of SVCO, accounting for up to 10% of the cases. In this scenario, the long smoking history, the hypercalcaemia and the chest examination, with right upper zone dullness and reduced entry, make lung cancer more likely.

Aortic aneurysm
The given scenario points towards a likely diagnosis of SVCO. In exploring the possible causes for this, it is important to consider patient’s risk factors, history and examination findings. The long history of smoking habit, together with the examination findings, suggests a malignant aetiology.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with haematuria. Investigations confirm the presence of a bladder carcinoma. In his occupational history, exposure to which one of the following substances would be a significant risk factor for his current diagnosis?
explanation:
Aromatic amines
Bladder carcinoma is associated with exposure to aromatic amines such as benzidine and beta-naphthylamine, which are sometimes used in the dye industry. Other risk factors include smoking – which is the most common cause and accounts for approximately half of all bladder cancers – and working in the rubber and leather industries.

Asbestos
Asbestos is incorrect. Asbestos increases the risk of lung cancer and in particular mesothelioma.

Arsenic
Arsenic is incorrect. Arsenic predisposes to skin cancer (squamous- and basal-cell carcinomas). It has been linked to bladder carcinoma but the risk is not as strong as aromatic amines.

Nickel
Nickel is incorrect. Nickel predisposes to squamous-cell carcinomas of the oral cavity.

Vinyl chloride.

stem: A 75-year-old heavy smoker of 40 cigarettes per day is admitted to the Emergency Department. He has a past history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. Over the past few months he has suffered a chronic cough and has lost approximately 2 stone (about 12.5 kg) in weight. He has been increasingly drowsy over the past few days and his relatives were unable to rouse him this morning. On examination he has a GCS of 6 and you notice that he has been incontinent of urine and faeces. What diagnosis fits with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Metastatic carcinoma with cerebral metastases
This man is a heavy smoker with a history of chronic cough and weight loss over the past few months, raising the possibility of bronchial carcinoma. The picture of progressively deteriorating conscious level points towards increasing cerebral oedema, almost certainly due to cerebral metastases from the bronchial tumour. This type of presentation is an indication for urgent computed tomography (CT) scanning. Treatment may include dexamethasone with or without mannitol IV to reduce cerebral oedema. Often deterioration of this nature is attributable to haemorrhage into an enlarging cerebral metastasis. Even if there is an initial response to medical treatment and conscious level improves, prognosis with this type of presentation is extremely poor. Around 50% of intracranial tumours are due to metastases, around 35% are due to malignant primary brain tumours (astrocytoma or oligodendroglioma), and around 10% are caused by benign brain tumours such as meningioma or neurofibroma.

Cerebral meningioma
Cerebral meningioma is incorrect. Cerebral meningioma is less common than metastatic carcinoma with cerebral metastases.

Embolic stroke
Embolic stroke is incorrect. Although embolic stroke is a possible alternative diagnosis given the history of atrial fibrillation, presentation would have been more acute.

Glioblastoma multiforme
Glioblastoma multiforme is incorrect. Primary brain tumours are less common than cerebral metastases.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage
Subarachnoid haemorrhage is incorrect. Subarachnoid haemorrhage would have a very acute presentation.

stem: A 69-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner (GP) with a 3-month history of bloating, fatigue, anorexia and depression. She also reports increasing abdominal pain and recent uterine bleeding. Her GP considers sending tumour markers. What is the most specific and sensitive tumour marker for ovarian cancer?
explanation:
Cancer antigen 125 (CA-125)
CA 125 is the only tumour marker recommended for clinical use in the diagnosis and management of ovarian cancer. The reference range of CA 125 is 0–35 units/ml (0–35 kU/l).

Prostate specific antigen (PSA)
This patient is a woman and PSA is used to help detect and to monitor prostate cancer.

Carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA)
CEA may be used to monitor the effect of treatment in colorectal cancer; it is also elevated, in a non-specific fashion, in the presence of certain cancers, eg pancreatic, prostate, ovary, lung, thyroid, and liver cancer.

Cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9)
CA 19-9 can be used to help tell the difference between cancer of the pancreas and bile ducts and other conditions; it can also be used to monitor the response to pancreatic cancer treatment and to watch for recurrence.

Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).

stem: A 40-year-old woman is worried about her risk of bowel cancer. Her father and two of her brothers all died from colorectal cancer in their 40s and 50s. Which other cancer would you specifically ask about in female relatives?
explanation:
Endometrial cancer
The family history is suggestive of a hereditary predisposition to bowel cancer, most probably hereditary, nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Approximately 70% of families with HNPCC have mutations in one of six known genes. The lifetime risk of developing colorectal cancer in affected individuals with HNPCC is 70–80% for men and 40–65% for women, with a mean age of onset of colorectal cancer at 44 years compared with 62 years in the general population. Affected females in HNPCC kindred have a 40–60% lifetime risk of developing endometrial cancer, so a history of endometrial cancers would further increase the likelihood that this is an HNPCC family. The risks for cancers of the small intestine, ureter, stomach, ovary and kidney can also be increased in HNPCC. Identifying such families is important as genetic testing is available and gene testing can be used to identify at-risk individuals who would benefit from colonoscopic screening.

Breast cancer
Breast cancer is incorrect. Hereditary breast cancer can be associated with a mutation in the BRCA genes, which can also cause ovarian, fallopian tube, prostate and pancreatic cancers.

Cervical cancer
Cervical cancer is incorrect. Cervical cancer is not commonly associated with hereditary syndromes.

Lung cancer
Lung cancer is incorrect. Lung cancer is not commonly associated with hereditary syndromes.

Vulval cancer.

stem: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) is most commonly associated with which tumour type?
explanation:
Small-cell carcinoma of the lung
SIADH is characterised by the abnormal release of ADH resulting in impaired water excretion with normal sodium excretion, which in turn leads to hyponatraemia and low plasma osmolality relative to urine osmolality. The most common malignant cause is small-cell lung cancer, but SIADH is also seen in carcinoid syndrome, pancreatic cancer, prostate cancer, lymphoma and leukaemia. It can also be caused by drugs (high-dose cyclophosphamide, vincristine), intracranial lesions and infections. Clinically it causes headaches, weakness, confusion, drowsiness and seizures.

Bronchial carcinoid tumour
Bronchial carcinoid tumour is incorrect. Bronchial carcinoid tumours are associated with the carcinoid syndrome.

Pancreatic cancer
Pancreatic cancer is incorrect. Pancreatic tumours of neuroendocrine origin may be associated with numerous hormonal syndromes depending on the cell of origin (ieglucagonoma, VIPoma, insulinoma).

Prostate cancer
Prostate cancer is incorrect. Prostate cancer may be associated with hypercalcaemia if skeletal metastases are present.

Squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung
Squamous-cell carcinoma of the lung is incorrect. Squamous-cell lung cancer may be associated with hypercalcaemia due to secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide.

stem: You are asked to review an 86-year-old patient on the ward who is complaining of abdominal pain. Upon review of his notes, you learn he has colon cancer and he has been admitted for severe constipation. He had been improving in the last few days, but he is still struggling with abdominal pain, mainly in the left iliac fossa. His current medications include senna, metformin, bisoprolol, clopidogrel and omeprazole. On examination, the abdomen is soft, but there is generalised discomfort on palpation, especially in the left iliac fossa. An abdominal X-ray shows faecal loading. What is the most appropriate management option to his symptoms?
options: Regular paracetamol and a phosphate enema
Paracetamol and codeine taken as needed (PRN)
explanation:
Regular paracetamol and a phosphate enema
According to the World Health Organisation's (WHO) 3-step pain relief ladder for cancer patients, it is advisable to try non-opiate drugs first with appropriate ‘adjuvants’. In this case, the enema will help with constipation and pain.

Paracetamol and codeine taken as needed (PRN)
Non-opiates should be trialled first and constipation should be addressed appropriately. Moreover, it is preferable to administer analgesia ‘by the clock’, rather than on patient’s demand.

Regular paracetamol and codeine
Regular opiates may exacerbate constipation. They may become necessary if pain is not well-controlled; however, non-opiates should be tried first.

Regular ibuprofen and PRN codeine
Ibuprofen should be used with caution – especially in elderly patients. In this case, a trial of regular paracetamol and addressing residual constipation is the best starting treatment among those available. Non-opiates should always be tried first, especially considering the potential of worsening constipation.

PRN oral morphine.

stem: A 55- year-old female with colon cancer has a tumour classified as ‘R2’. What does the R2 classification stand for in cancer therapy?
options: The tumour was macroscopically visible but could not be removed completely
explanation:
The tumour was macroscopically visible but could not be removed completely
The following residual tumour (R) classification exists in addition to the TNM classification and the histological grade (G): RX presence of residual tumour cannot be assessed R0 no residual tumour R1 microscopic residual tumour R2 macroscopic residual tumour. Tumour size, lymph node involvement and metastasis presence are indicated by the T, N and M classifications, respectively.

Lymph-node involvement
Lymph-node involvement is incorrect. Lymph node involvement is indicated by the N classification.

Metastases present
Metastases present is incorrect. Metastasis presence is indicated by the M classification.

Tumour size 2 cm
Tumour size is incorrect. Tumour size is indicated by the T classification.

Well-differentiated tumour
Well-differentiated tumour is incorrect. Tumour differentiation is included in the grading classification rather than staging.

stem: An 89-year-old man with advanced prostatic cancer presents to hospital with malaise and lethargy. On examination, he is extremely cachectic and he reports a loss of weight of about 8 kg in about a month. Which of these parameters would you most expect to be elevated in a patient with cachexia and metastatic cancer?
explanation:
C-reactive protein
There is a well-described correlation between acute-phase reactive proteins (such as C-reactive protein, albumin, interleukin (IL)1A, IL1B, IL6, IL8, IL10, tumour necrosis factor (TNF)-A, midkine, vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-A, VEGF-C, leptin, adiponectin, and ghrelin). Patients with cachexia often carry high levels of certain acute phase proteins, which also appears to be associated with tumour burden. C-reactive protein is commonly increased in patients with advanced cancer and especially in those with cachexia.

Sodium levels
Sodium levels may be elevated in cancer patients for several reasons: for example: dehydration ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) production increased diuresis (eg in hypercalcaemia) medications (eg sulfonylureas). The presence of cachexia would make C-reactive protein the most appropriate answer, as this is an acute phase protein and it is usually increased in cancer patients with cachexia.

Platelets
Platelets may be elevated in any inflammatory conditions; however, in this scenario and in view of cachexia, Creactive protein would most likely be elevated.

Anti-diuretic hormone (ADH) levels
ADH is not routinely measured as conditions related to its excessive production/deficiency are diagnosed through clinical features and other laboratory tests (such as electrolytes and osmolality). Patients with certain types of cancer – most frequently, lung cancer and lymphoma – can develop syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH) secretion. This would manifest with hyponatraemia, which can cause a spectrum of symptoms from nausea/vomiting to seizure, stupor and coma. In a man with cachexia, acute phase proteins will be raised, so C-reactive protein is the correct answer in this case.

Urea
Patients with cancer may have raised urea secondary to dehydration, increased cell turnover or kidney injury. In this scenario, the presence of cachexia and rapid weight loss are associated with increase of acute phase protein, such as C-reactive protein, IL1A, IL1B, IL6, IL8, IL10, TNF-A, midkine, VEGF-A, VEGF-C, leptin, adiponectin, and ghrelin.

stem: Which one of the following would be most appropriate to provide a definitive diagnosis?
options: Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of thyroid nodule
explanation:
Fine-needle aspiration biopsy of thyroid nodule
The main suspicion in this scenario is that the patient has a malignant thyroid tumour. This is mainly based on the persisting cough, in absence of relevant chest findings on chest X-ray and examination, and the presence of a firm non-tender thyroid nodule. In addition, his age and smoking history both constitute risk factors. In order to reach a definite diagnosis, a histological sample needs to be obtained, therefore, the recommended first-line investigation would be a fine-needle aspiration biopsy of the nodule.

Ultrasound scan (USS) of thyroid
An USS of the thyroid is useful to further assess the features of a thyroid nodule and also to characterise the neck lymph node; however, this would not provide a definite diagnosis. This can only be sought via a sample analysis to reach a pathological diagnosis.

Computed tomography (CT) head and neck
In this scenario, the main concern is an underlying thyroid cancer. Imaging of the neck, like an US in the first instance, is certainly useful; however it would not provide histological confirmation and therefore does not constitute the best option in this case.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) neck
An MRI neck may give useful information about the thyroid nodule and the surrounding tissues; however, this would not provide a definite diagnosis and also would not offer much more than a USS thyroid, which would be the preferred imaging choice.

Excisional lymph node biopsy
Given the longstanding dry cough, coupled with the features of the thyroid nodule on examination, the primary differential diagnosis would be that of a thyroid malignancy. Therefore, an excisional lymph node biopsy is not appropriate in this case, where the histological sample has to be collected from the thyroid.

stem: Which of the following investigations is most useful to reach a diagnosis?
explanation:
Oesophageal-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD)
The described appearance of the skin lesions with hyperpigmented velvety symmetrical patches and thickened skin is typical of acanthosis nigricans (AN). AN is thought to be caused by a variety of different mechanism, but there is general consensus about the involvement of tyrosine growth factor receptor signalling pathways. AN can be associated with different pathologies or may be drug induced. A common association has been observed between obesity, diabetes and in general insulin resistance. The malignant form usually appears in people older than 40 years of age, without any family associations. In the majority of cases, malignant AN is associated with abdominal neoplasm, especially GI ones. It tends to progress rapidly and may follows the underlaying cancer progression. The presence of itchiness and tenderness is typical of malignant AN and therefore should be seriously considered when approaching the underlaying clinical diagnosis. The case describes several red flags for a probable GI malignancy: dysphagia, retrosternal chest pain, lethargy, malnutrition, cachexia and presence of risk factors (age, previous tobacco use and GI reflux). Therefore, an urgent OGD should be arranged, which would allow a histological diagnosis on tissue biopsies.

Skin biopsy
The most likely underlaying diagnosis is cancer of the upper gastrointestinal tract with associated AN. AN is not characterised by malignant cells infiltration, therefore a skin biopsy would not clarify the underlaying diagnosis.

Autoimmune screen
Because the patient has dysphagia, loss of weight, lethargy, cachexia and evidence of malnutrition, coupled with previous tobacco use and gastrointestinal reflux, there is a strong suspicion for underlaying upper GI malignancy.

Computed tomography (CT) chest/abdomen/pelvis
The most likely underlaying diagnosis is cancer of the upper GI tract with associated AN. A CT chest/abdomen/pelvis may reveal the presence of the underlying malignancy and provide staging; however, this would not allow for taking of biopsies for histological confirmation. An OGD should be performed in the first instance.

Fasting plasma glucose (FPG)
Diabetes can be associated with AN; however, in this case, the symptoms described point towards malignant AN, warranting urgent investigation of the upper GI tract.

stem: You are attending a meeting where the introduction of a new screening programme to detect early lung cancer is being discussed. Which one of the following is the most important criterion when deciding whether such a programme should be introduced?
options: A clinically effective and cost-effective method of early treatment
Current technology makes early detection possible
The cost per patient found of a screening programme
explanation:
A clinically effective and cost-effective method of early treatment
The type of screening in this question is concerned with the detection of a disease, in this case lung cancer, at its earliest stage to maximise the possibility of cure. Screening programmes for a particular disease should not necessarily be introduced merely because it is technically possible to detect the condition at an earlier stage – there has to be evidence that early diagnosis will affect the outcome for the patient. The other answers are all valid aspects that need to be assessed once clinical benefit has been established. The specificity of a test is a measure of its ability to correctly identify healthy people as not having the disease, and therefore a highly specific test would give a low number of false-positives. The sensitivity of a test is a measure of its ability to detect the disease when it is present, and therefore a highly sensitive test would have very few or no missed cases. Randomised controlled trials are currently being conducted to determine whether improved detection by techniques such as spiral CT will translate into reduced lung cancer mortality rates.

Current technology makes early detection possible
Current technology makes early detection possible is incorrect. As described, the key issue is of improved outcome as a result of early diagnosis.

The cost per patient found of a screening programme
The cost per patient found of a screening programme is incorrect. As described, the key issue is of improved outcome as a result of early diagnosis.

The sensitivity of the test
The sensitivity of the test is incorrect. As described, the key issue is of improved outcome as a result of early diagnosis.

The specificity of the test
The specificity of the test is incorrect. As described, the key issue is of improved outcome as a result of early diagnosis.

stem: What is the most appropriate systemic therapy to be given with concurrent radiotherapy?
explanation:
Cisplatin and etoposide
Standard chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer remains cisplatin and etoposide, but carboplatin is frequently used in patients who cannot tolerate or who have a contraindication to cisplatin. However, this area of medicine is subject to rapid change as immunotherapy has already started to alter the management of advanced small cell lung cancer; this may soon be extended to limited small cell lung cancer, as in this case.

Carboplatin and etoposide
This is a second-line option in the treatment of small cell lung cancer. The combination of cisplatin and etoposide is only replaced by carboplatin and etoposide in patients who cannot tolerate or who have a contraindication to cisplatin.

Carboplatin and paclitaxel
Carboplatin and paclitaxel is a treatment option for non-small cell lung cancer as opposed to small cell lung cancer.

Topotecan and ifosfamide
Topotecan and ifosfamide have activity in relapsed small cell lung cancer.

Vinorelbine and cisplatin
Vinorelbine and cisplatin are used in non-small cell lung cancer. This patient has small cell lung cancer.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with postcoital bleeding and pelvic pain. She has a history of irregular menstrual cycles and has not had a cervical smear test in over five years. On examination, there is an ulcerated lesion on the cervix. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Invasive cervical cancer
Invasive cervical cancer is the most likely diagnosis, given the patient's symptoms of postcoital bleeding, pelvic pain, and an ulcerated lesion on the cervix observed during examination. These symptoms are highly suggestive of advanced disease, especially in someone who has not had regular screening via smear tests, which could have detected pre-cancerous changes early. The presence of an ulcerated lesion further indicates invasive disease rather than benign conditions such as polyps or ectropion. Cervical cancer can be confirmed through biopsy and imaging studies.

Cervical ectropion
While cervical ectropion can cause postcoital bleeding due to exposure of glandular cells from inside the cervix on its outer surface, it commonly presents with excessive vaginal discharge. Upon examination. It generally appears as a red area around the os rather than an ulcerative area.

Cervical polyp
Polyps may cause irregular spotting or postcoital bleeding but are usually asymptomatic otherwise and do not generally lead to significant pelvic pain or appear as ulcerative lesions upon inspection. They tend to be small growths protruding from the endocervical canal.

Cervicitis
This condition involves inflammation of the cervix, often due to infection (eg chlamydia or gonorrhoea). Although it can cause abnormal vaginal discharge and some degree of discomfort during intercourse, it typically does not present with significant postcoital bleeding combined with severe pelvic pain or visible ulceration akin to what might be seen in invasive malignancy.

stem: A 34-year-old patient with motor neurone disease is admitted with type 2 respiratory failure. He has chosen to die from respiratory insufficiency and does not want any intervention, having stated this in writing on two previous admissions and completed an advanced decision in conjunction with NHS guidance. His breathing deteriorates and he becomes confused. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Relatives to sign informed consent for ventilation
Relieve any respiratory distress with opiates or other respiratory suppressants
explanation:
Relieve any respiratory distress with opiates or other respiratory suppressants
Advanced decision documentation, as long as it is completed by a patient who is deemed to have mental capacity, and it is appropriately signed and witnessed, is legally binding. As such, in this case it’s important to abide by the patient’s wishes.

Relatives to sign informed consent for ventilation
Relatives to sign informed consent for ventilation is incorrect. It is important to bear in mind that judgement may be clouded at times of significant stress such as this, and there is the potential that the patient’s relatives could go against their express wishes. As such, they should be informed and discussions should take place, but they should not influence the level of intervention.

Ventilation without the patient’s permission
Ventilation without the patient’s permission is incorrect. Given the patient’s express wishes not to be ventilated, this could be considered assault, and is therefore not appropriate.Hydrocortisone but no ventilation
Hydrocortisone but no ventilation is incorrect. Hydrocortisone does not have a role in relieving distress, and should therefore not be instituted. Useful external weblinks NHS: end of life care (related to - Relieve any respiratory distress with opiates or other respiratory suppressants) www.nhs.uk/Planners/end-of-life-care/Pages/advance-decision-to-refuse-treatment.aspx.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the Respiratory Clinic with recurrent haemoptysis. A well-defined, rounded lesion within the right middle lobe has been identified on chest X-ray arranged by the General Practitioner. He smokes five cigarettes per day and has no significant past medical history. Examination reveals a blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg; pulse is 70 bpm and regular. There are no murmurs on auscultation; there is some wheeze over the right middle lobe. His abdomen is soft and non-tender. Routine bloods including liver function tests are unremarkable. Which of the following is the most useful pointer to the likely diagnosis here?
explanation:
Chromogranin A
The most likely underlying diagnosis, given the history and X-ray findings, is bronchial carcinoid. Out of the options listed, both elevated chromogranin A and neuron-specific enolase are seen in conjunction with carcinoid, although chromogranin A is the more sensitive of the two markers.

Alpha fetoprotein
Alpha fetoprotein is seen with hepatocellular carcinoma

Serum carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9
CA 19-9 is seen in pancreatic carcinoma.

Carcino-embryonic antigen (CEA)
CEA is seen with predominantly right-sided colon cancer, lung and breast cancer.

Neuron-specific enolase
Although neuron-specific enolase is seen in conjunction with carcinoid, of it and chromogranin A it is the less sensitive, making this the better answer.

stem: An 81-year-old man presents to Emergency Department with retrosternal chest pain. He has a past medical history of ischaemic heart disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), osteoarthritis and prostatism. His medications are aspirin, omeprazole, paracetamol, ibuprofen and tamsulosin. The patient reports a 6-month history of recurrent chest pains. He has also experienced difficulty with swallowing which he overcomes by eating soft food. As a consequence, he has lost 7 kg in weight. A gastro-duodenoscopy is performed and a histological sample is retrieved from an exophytic mass in the distal oesophagus, which is reported as follows: ‘Moderately differentiated tubo-papillary growth with mucinous differentiation. This invades beyond muscolaris mucosae.’ What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Oesophageal adenocarcinoma
The most significant risk factors for oesophageal adenocarcinoma are symptomatic GORD, obesity, Barrett’s oesophagus, tobacco use and a diet low in vegetables and fruit. GORD is considered one of the strongest risk factors. Endoscopically, if detected early, these tumours will present as mucosal irregularities. In later stages, they appear as ulcerated/infiltrative or exophytic masses with obstruction. Histologically, these are gland-forming tumours with a tubular, tubule-papillary or papillary growth pattern. A small subset of cases shows mucinous differentiation. In this case, the patient has a suggestive history, significant risk factors and typical histology, therefore, oesophageal adenocarcinoma is the most likely diagnosis.

Invasive squamous cell carcinoma (SCC)
The histological features in SCC are different from those described in this scenario. It is not characterised by intestinal transformation and gland patterned proliferation. Well-differentiated SCC show presence of keratin pearls, cell keratinisation and intercellular bridges. Risk factors for SCC are tobacco use, alcohol consumption, mutations of enzymes that metabolise alcohol, achalasia, caustic injury, history of thoracic radiation, low socioeconomic status, poor oral hygiene, nutritional deficiencies and non-epidermolytic palmoplantar keratoderma.

Barrett’s oesophagus (BE)
In BE, the squamous mucosa is replaced by columnar epithelium, and upper-oesophageal endoscopy shows a salmon-coloured mucosa which extends in caudo-cephalic fashion. GORD and bile reflux are risk factors for BE. This is because reflux injures the normal squamous mucosa, and BE is thought to be a protective adaption. In this case, the invasion beyond the muscolaris mucosae rules out BE, which is not associated with invasive features.

Intramucosal adenocarcinoma
The histological description of the biopsy sample taken from distal oesophagus is described as invasive beyond muscolaris mucosa; therefore, it is not considered intramucosal anymore. The feature described are in keeping with moderately differentiated adenocarcinoma.

Non-invasive SCC
SCC carries different histological features, which vary according to the degree of differentiation. In general, it is characterised by growth of epithelial squamous cells, sometimes showing degree of keratinisation and intercellular bridges.

stem: Which malignancy is currently the number one cause of death in women in the United Kingdom (UK)?
explanation:
Lung cancer
Cancer is the cause of 26% of deaths in the UK, and is a more common cause of death than cardiovascular disease. Lung cancer, with its low survival rates, is the biggest cancer killer in the UK, although breast cancer has the highest incidence. In 2018 over one-fifth (21%) of all cancer deaths in women were from lung cancer, 15% from breast cancer, 10% from colon cancer. Leukaemia and uterine cancer are rarer, each accounting for approximately 3% of cancer deaths in women. In males the most common cause of cancer death is also lung cancer (21%), with prostate (13%) and colon cancer (10%) also causing significant mortality. On average 92 people die every day from lung cancer in the UK. Cigarette smoking has been identified as the single most important cause of preventable disease and premature death in the UK. Overall, one-third of all cancer deaths are linked to smoking.

Breast cancer
Breast cancer is incorrect. Although, as described, breast cancer has the highest incidence, it accounts for 15% of cancer deaths in women compared to 26% for lung cancer.

Colon cancer
Colon cancer is incorrect. Colon cancer accounted for approximately 9% of cancer deaths in women.

Leukaemia
Leukaemia is incorrect. Leukaemia accounted for approximately 3% of cancer deaths in women.

Uterine cancer
Uterine cancer is incorrect. Uterine cancer accounted for approximately 3% of cancer deaths in women.

stem: A 57-year-old man complains of nausea, abdominal pain and fatigue. Screening blood tests indicate hypercalcaemia. He is referred to hospital and cross-sectional imaging demonstrates metastatic malignancy of uncertain origin. No obvious bony metastases are demonstrated. Hypercalcaemia in malignant disease secondary to the secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP) by the tumour is most frequently associated with which one of the following?
explanation:
Squamous-cell carcinoma of the bronchus
Hypercalcaemia is a frequent complication of cancer, and is frequently the result of the secretion of parathyroid hormone related peptide (PTHrP). Squamous cell carcinomas of the bronchus are most frequently responsible, although hypercalcaemia is not uncommon with other bronchogenic cancers (including small-cell carcinoma, option D). PTHrP simulates most of the actions of PTH, including increases in bone resorption and distal tubular calcium reabsorption, and inhibition of proximal tubular phosphate transport. However, it does not increase intestinal calcium absorption.

Carcinoid tumours
Carcinoid tumours is incorrect. Carcinoid tumours sometimes secrete vasopressin or ACTH, but rarely cause hypercalcaemia.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. In lymphomas unregulated extrarenal production of calcitriol can be responsible.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. In myeloma the secretion of osteoclast activating cytokines is the usual cause of hypercalcaemia.

Small-cell carcinoma of the bronchus.

stem: A 72-year-old heavy smoker presents with shortness of breath and haemoptysis. On examination you notice some facial swelling. You suspect a bronchial neoplasm. What other clinical sign would it be particularly important to look for if you were suspecting superior vena caval (SVC) obstruction?
options: Venous dilatation over the anterior chest wall
explanation:
Venous dilatation over the anterior chest wall
Venous dilatation over the anterior chest wall is a typical sign that may occur with SVC obstruction. This man is a heavy smoker in which a bronchial neoplasm is suspected and there is associated facial swelling. This should suggest SVC obstruction. This is an oncological emergency and can be treated with radiotherapy or steroids.

Central cyanosis
Central cyanosis is incorrect. Central cyanosis may occur in patients with lung cancer but is not useful in deciding whether SVC obstruction is present or not.

Finger clubbing
Finger clubbing is incorrect. Finger clubbing may suggest an underlying bronchial neoplasm, but once again does not point to underlying SVC obstruction.

Horner's syndrome
Horner’s syndrome is incorrect. Horner’s syndrome would be another complication of an upper lobe neoplasm, but would not point specifically towards SVC obstruction.

Supraclavicular or cervical lymphadenopathy.

stem: What is the most likely sequela of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma?
explanation:
Upper airway obstruction
Anaplastic carcinoma is the rarest of all thyroid tumours (<1%). Cervical lymph node metastases are present in 90% at diagnosis, lung metastases in 50% and tracheal invasion in 25%. Anaplastic carcinoma has a very poor prognosis with a median survival of 4–5 months. The most common sequela is upper airway obstruction. Surgery has a limited role in relieving obstructive symptoms; external beam radiotherapy is useful in palliation. The role of chemotherapy (usually doxorubicin combined with other drugs) is unclear. Many patients will require a tracheostomy to manage airway obstruction. Brain and liver metastases may occur but are not common. Bone, lung and cervical lymph node metastases are common. Hypercalcaemia is not a feature of anaplastic thyroid cancer unless secondary to bone metastases. In medullary thyroid cancer, calcium metabolism can be disordered owing to elevated levels of calcitonin secreted by the tumour.

Brain metastasis
Brain metastasis is incorrect. Brain metastases may occur but they are not common.

Good prognosis
Good prognosis is incorrect. Anaplastic carcinoma has a very poor prognosis with a median survival of 4–5 months.

Hypercalcaemia
Hypercalcaemia is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia is not a feature of anaplastic thyroid cancer unless secondary to bone metastases.

Liver metastasis
Liver metastasis is incorrect. Liver metastases may occur but they are not common.

stem: In which part of the cell cycle are cells most resistant to cytotoxic chemotherapy?
explanation:
G 0 phase
The cell cycle is an ordered set of events, culminating in cell growth and division into two daughter cells. G 0 phase (resting stage) Cells have not yet started to divide. This step can last for a few hours to a few years. When the cell is signalled to reproduce, it moves into the G 1 phase. G 1 phase During this phase, the cell starts making more proteins to get ready to divide. This phase lasts about 20–30 h. S phase In S phase, the DNA is copied. This phase lasts about 15–20 h. G 2 phase The G 2 phase is just before the cell mitosis. It lasts 2–10 h. M phase (mitosis) In this phase, which lasts only 30–60 min, the cell divides. Many chemotherapy drugs work only on actively reproducing cells (not on cells in the resting phase, G 0). Most chemotherapy agents specifically attack cells in a particular phase of the cell cycle (the M or S phases, for example). This principle is used in combination chemotherapy where drugs that act on different phases of the cell cycle are combined to maximise the anti-tumour effect. Multiple cycles of treatment are utilised in chemotherapy regimens in order to maximise the population of cells targeted. Examples of agents targeting each portion of the cell cycle are as follows: methotrexiate, 5-flurouracil: S phase; bleomycin: G 2 phase; docetaxel: M phase; etoposide: G 1 phase. Other agents (eg cyclophosphamide) are not cell cycle specific and can affect cells at any stage. Understanding of the cell cycle explains why chemotherapy toxicity mainly affects rapidly growing normal tissues (eg gastrointestinal mucosa, bone marrow) as these are less likely to be in G 0 compared with other tissues.

G 1 phase
G 1 phase is incorrect. Cells not in the resting phase are more susceptible to chemotherapy.

G 2 phase
G 2 phase is incorrect. Cells not in the resting phase are more susceptible to chemotherapy.

M phase
M phase is incorrect. Cells not in the resting phase are more susceptible to chemotherapy.

S phase
S phase is incorrect. Cells not in the resting phase are more susceptible to chemotherapy.

stem: A 65-year-old hospice-resident with metastatic breast cancer presents with a 24-hour history of bilateral leg weakness and severe lower back pain. Her background includes ischaemic heart disease, type II diabetes and fibromyalgia. She has had one episode of urinary incontinence on her way to the hospital. On examination, she showed decreased power on both legs and reduced anal tone. There is mid-spine tenderness on palpation of her lower spine. What is the best management option for this patient’s symptoms?
options: Await Palliative Care Team review for symptoms management
Discharge the patient back to the Hospice with subcutaneous (SC) morphine
No treatment until magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) whole spine is performed to confirm diagnosis
explanation:
Oral dexamethasone and analgesia
The described scenario offers several red flags for possible spinal cord compression, most likely secondary to metastatic deposit in the spine from breast cancer. While waiting for further investigations to confirm diagnosis, the recommended treatment includes oral dexamethasone, along with appropriate analgesia according to the World Health Organisation (WHO) 3-step pain relief ladder. Proton pump inhibitors should also be prescribed for gastric protection. If not contraindicated, an MRI whole-spine should be carried out. A multi-disciplinary discussion with Oncology and Palliative Care team should take place to propose a suitable plan in the context of advanced cancer as the patient may be suitable for further treatment such as stabilisation surgery or palliative radiotherapy.

Ibuprofen
The suspected diagnosis in this case is metastatic spinal cord compression. Ibuprofen alone is unlikely to offer good symptoms control in this case and oral dexamethasone should be administered, along with appropriate analgesia.

Await Palliative Care Team review for symptoms management
This patient has advanced breast cancer and suspected spinal cord compression. Palliative Care Team input may not be immediately available, leaving the patient in severe discomfort, therefore, initial steps for suspected spinal cord compression should be taken, while awaiting further investigation.

Discharge the patient back to the Hospice with subcutaneous (SC) morphine
The likely diagnosis in this case is metastatic spinal cord compression, in the presence of metastatic breast cancer. Considering the advanced stage of the tumour, the main focus should be to maintain the best quality of life possible. SC morphine alone may be effective in reducing pain, but this would not influence the oedema/inflammation triggered by cord compression. Failing to act upon mentioned red flags may result in para or tetraplegia.

No treatment until magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) whole spine is performed to confirm diagnosis
Though it is important to confirm the diagnosis of metastatic spinal cord compression with imaging, in a patient with advanced cancer, it is important to address symptoms control in timely manner. Therefore, while waiting for further investigations, the recommended treatment should include oral dexamethasone, along with appropriate analgesia according to WHO 3-step pain relief ladder.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with breast cancer underwent a wide local excision for an invasive ductal carcinoma two years ago. She now presents to the Emergency Department with confusion, lethargy and thigh pain. X-ray reveals a cystic lesion in the shaft of the femur. Her calcium level is 3.5 mmol/l. Which one of the following is the next step in her therapy?
explanation:
Saline infusion
The acute management of hypercalcaemia involves general measures to enhance hydration and diuresis, and specific measures using drugs to lower serum calcium. Dehydration due to hypercalcaemic symptoms, for example anorexia, nausea, vomiting and polyuria because of defective urinary concentration, is very common and patients may require 5–10 litres of 0.9% sodium chloride over a period of 24–48 hours. This vigorous hydration with normal salinemay lower the serum calcium concentration by 0.25–0.75 mmol/l, and also enhances urinary calcium excretion by increasing glomerular filtration and reducing the proximal and distal renal tubular reabsorption of calcium and sodium. A loop diuretic, for example, furosemide 20–100 mg, may be required to control complications due to volume overload, especially in the elderly and those with impaired cardiovascular and renal function. Large-volume saline diuresis may lead to hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and electrolyte imbalance, which will need correction. If saline diuresis is unsuccessful, and particularly if the hypercalcaemia is severe, then more specific measures, for example bisphosphonates or renal dialysis, may be required.

Glucocorticoids
Glucocorticoids is incorrect. Glucocorticoids may be indicated to control pain secondary to the bone metastasis but will not correct serum calcium.

Tamoxifen treatment
Tamoxifen treatment is incorrect. Tamoxifen may play a role in the long-term management of her metastatic breast cancer but is not indicated acutely to correct hypercalcaemia.

Urgent orthopaedic referral
Urgent orthopaedic referral is incorrect. Orthopaedic review should be considered to assess the risk of fracture, but management of malignant hypercalcaemia should be under the supervision of the oncology team.

Urgent radiotherapy
Urgent radiotherapy is incorrect. Radiotherapy may be indicated to control pain secondary to the bone metastasis but will not correct serum calcium. Calcium Homeostasis,.

stem: Which of the following is the most probable cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Small-cell lung cancer
Small-cell lung cancer is associated with smoking and usually develops in the hilar region of the lung. It is aggressive, rapidly metastases and is responsible for ectopic production of both adrenocorticotrophic hormone (ACTH) and antidiuretic hormone (ADH). In this case, the low sodium is a pointer towards the syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion (SIADH), especially given the absence of any signs of fluid overload, orAI renal Tutoror hepatic dysfunction. Symptoms of SIADH resolve as treatment is instituted for the underlying lung tumour.

Adenocarcinoma of the bronchus
Adenocarcinoma of the bronchus is not linked to cigarette smoking and is not associated with ectopic production of antidiuretic hormone and consequent hyponatraemia.

Bronchial carcinoid
Bronchial carcinoid is associated with recurrent haemoptysis and bronchial obstruction. It is not linked to smoking and is generally seen in younger patients.

Large-cell lung cancer
Large-cell lung cancer is a poorly differentiated aggressive form of lung cancer. It is not responsible for ectopic hormone production and is therefore unlikely to be the cause of this patient’s hyponatraemia.

Squamous cell lung cancer
Squamous cell lung cancer is responsible for production of parathyroid hormone (PTH)-related peptide, which leads to hypercalcaemia. It doesn’t fit with the picture of SIADH seen here.

stem: A 64-year-old man with a long history of smoking presents to the Emergency Department following a fracture of his left humerus associated with a very minor twisting injury. On reviewing the films with the on-call radiographer you are concerned about a lytic lesion possibly being related to the fracture. Which one of the following primary tumours is this patient likely to have?
explanation:
Bronchial carcinoma
The most common tumours causing bone metastasis include: bronchial carcinoma, breast carcinoma and prostatic carcinoma. Metastases to bone also typically occur from renal or thyroid carcinomas, but as these tumours are less common, bony metastases of these origins are less often seen. Colorectal and gastric carcinomas may metastasise to bone, but more commonly involve viscera such as liver or lungs. Primary bone tumours (such as osteosarcomas, fibrosarcomas and chondromas) are rare and usually only seen in children and young adults. Symptoms are usually related to the primary tumour site, with local bone pain unless patients present with a pathological fracture as in this case. X-ray examination reveals osteolytic areas and local bony destruction. Osteosclerotic metastases are characteristic of prostatic carcinoma.

Colorectal carcinoma
Colorectal carcinoma is incorrect. Colorectal carcinomas may metastasise to bone, but more commonly involve viscera such as liver or lungs.

Gastric carcinoma
Gastric carcinoma is incorrect. Gastric carcinomas may metastasise to bone, but more commonly involve viscera such as liver or lungs.

Renal carcinoma
Renal carcinoma is incorrect. Although renal carcinoma may metastasise to bone, as it is less common than bronchial cancer it is not the most likely cause here.

Thyroid carcinoma
Thyroid carcinoma is incorrect. Although thyroid carcinoma may metastasise to bone, as it is less common than bronchial cancer it is not the most likely cause here.

stem: You are taking part in a trial of a monoclonal antibody that is thought to modulate the acute phase response. The sponsor plans to measure a range of acute phase proteins. Which of the following is a recognised positive acute phase protein?
explanation:
Ferritin
Ferritin is a recognised acute phase protein. Therefore, it is increased in inflammatory and infective conditions. Consequently, this may mask the diagnosis of iron deficiency if there are co-existing inflammatory or neoplastic states.

Albumin
Albumin is incorrect. While albumin is an acute phase protein it is in fact a negative acute phase protein i.e. it decreases in an acute phase response.

C-peptide
C-peptide is incorrect. C-peptide is not an acute phase protein – this is a cleavage product of proinsulin.

IL-10
IL-10 is incorrect. Interleukin 10 is not an acute phase protein, but is a cytokine which induces a T-cell response.

Relaxin
Relaxin is incorrect. Relaxin is a hormone produced during pregnancy which leads to arteriolar dilatation.

stem: A 73-year-old man with prostate cancer is under the management of the oncology clinic. Which one of the following laboratory tests is most useful for screening and therapy control in this patient?
explanation:
Prostate-specific antigen
The introduction of the prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test has led to increasing public awareness of prostate cancer, and, as a consequence, diagnosis is increasingly made before metastases into lymph nodes or bone are evident. Bone metastases are very unlikely unless the PSA exceeds 20 ng/ml, and a bone scan at diagnosis is unnecessary in patients whose PSA is below 20 ng/ml. Large numbers of cancers are now diagnosed following a PSA test at a stage before they are palpable (category T1c) by transrectal ultrasound biopsy. The usual indication for biopsy is a PSA exceeding 4 ng/ml. PSA is also useful for monitoring response to therapy in patients with carcinoma of the prostate.

α-Fetoprotein
Alpha-fetoprotein is incorrect. Alpha-fetoprotein is used in the management of germ cell tumours and hepatocellular carcinomas.

Alkaline phosphatase
Alkaline phosphatase is incorrect. Alkaline phosphatase is a marker for germ cell tumours and bony metastases from any malignancy.

Carcinoembryonic antigen
Carcinoembryonic antigen is incorrect. Carcinoembryonic antigen is a marker for colorectal cancer.

Lactate dehydrogenase.

stem: A 68-year-old man attends a Well Man clinic with his GP. He is noted to have non-visible haematuria, an ESR of 75mm and serum calcium of 3.12 mmol/l, with elevated ALP; his eGFR is 76ml/min/1.73m 2. On examination, he appears to have a varicocele. Which one of the following diagnoses fits best with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Renal cell adenocarcinoma
Renal cell adenocarcinoma makes up 3% of all adult malignancies, with peak incidence being 50–70 years; there is a male-to-female preponderance of 2 : 1. Varicocele, resulting from obstruction of venous drainage, is found in 2–3% of cases. Haematuria is the presenting feature in 50–60% of cases. Raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) is found in 50–60% of cases. Hypercalcaemia occurs due to raised parathyroid hormone-related protein (PTHrP) in around 3% of cases. The most common sites of metastases are lung (50– 60%) and bone (30–40%). The treatment of choice is nephrectomy. Prognosis is related to tumour staging: the 5-year survival rate is around 80–100% in those with TNM stage 1 lesions, but this falls to 5–10% in those with stage 4 lesions.

Retroperitoneal sarcoma
Retroperitoneal sarcoma is incorrect. Retroperitoneal sarcomas are very rare and do not originate from renal tissue. It would not be expected to present with haematuria.

Secondary hyperparathyroidism
Secondary hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. Secondary hyperparathyroidism is unlikely in a patient without chronic kidney disease (CKD). It may also be seen in other causes of hypocalcaemia, such as malabsorption of fat-soluble vitamin D, due to chronic pancreatitis or after bariatric surgery.

Urinary tract infection (UTI)
Urinary tract infection (UTI) is incorrect. UTI does not routinely cause hypercalcaemia.

Wilms’ tumour
Wilms’ tumour is incorrect. Wilms’ tumour is rare in adults.

stem: A 57-year-old man presents with weight loss and a neck swelling. He is subsequently confirmed to have a thyroid malignancy. Which one of the following statements regarding this condition is correct?
options: Iodine-131 therapy is an alternative to total thyroidectomy
Papillary cell carcinoma of the thyroid produces high calcitonin levels
Serum thyroglobulin measurement is the main method of early detection of recurrent papillary and
Subtotal lobectomy is the minimum treatment of choice
explanation:
Serum thyroglobulin measurement is the main method of early detection of recurrent papillary and
Serum thyroglobulin measurement is the main method of early detection of recurrent papillary and follicular thyroid cancers Thyroglobulin, a glycoprotein, is produced by normal and neoplastic follicular cells. Serum thyroglobulin measurements are the main modality for the early detection of recurrent differentiated (papillary/follicular) thyroid cancer.

80–90% are medullary carcinomas
80–90% are medullary carcinomas is incorrect. Papillary (80–85%) and follicular (5–10%) carcinomas account for 80–90% of thyroid cancers. Medullary and anaplastic thyroid tumours are rarer.

Iodine-131 therapy is an alternative to total thyroidectomy
Iodine-131 therapy is an alternative to total thyroidectomy is incorrect. Iodine-131 destroys the residual normal thyroid tissue following resection. To maximise therapy, a total or near-total thyroidectomy should be performed in all patients who are to be treated with iodine.

Papillary cell carcinoma of the thyroid produces high calcitonin levels
Papillary cell carcinoma of the thyroid produces high calcitonin levels is incorrect. Calcitonin is produced by C cells in medullary carcinoma.

Subtotal lobectomy is the minimum treatment of choice
Subtotal lobectomy is the minimum treatment of choice is incorrect. Total lobectomy is the minimum treatment for thyroid cancer.

stem: A 30-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 2 is under surveillance for the development of intracranial malignancy. Which nervous system tumour typically manifests bilaterally in patients with neurofibromatosis type 2?
explanation:
Acoustic neuroma
The gene for neurofibromatosis type 2 (central neurofibromatosis) has been mapped to chromosome 22q12.2. This disorder is characterised by bilateral acoustic neuromas, but tumours may occur on other cranial nerves or spinal roots and also paraspinally. Meningiomas and gliomas may also develop. A further feature is the occurrence of juvenile posterior subcapsular lenticular opacities.

Capillary haemangioma
Capillary haemangioma is incorrect. Capillary haemangioma is a benign vascular abnormality most commonly occurring in infants (‘strawberry birthmark’).

Ependymoma of the ventricles
Ependymoma of the ventricles is incorrect. Ependymomas may be a feature of neurofibromatosis, but are not typically bilateral.

Giant-cell astrocytoma
Giant-cell astrocytoma is incorrect. Giant-cell astrocytoma is a brain tumour associated with the tuberous sclerosis syndrome.

stem: A 37-year-old man has a lump in his testicle, a mass on chest X-ray and a raised β-HCG. Which one of the following would be the most appropriate next step in his management?
options: CT-guided biopsy of the chest lesion
explanation:
Staging computed tomography (CT) scan
The triad of a testicular lump, a mass on chest X-ray and a raised β-HCG (human chorionic gonadotrophin) are suggestive of testicular seminoma. A raised β-HCG is found in around 15% of seminomas and may be a useful correlate with response to treatment. ‘Pure’ seminoma will not be associated with a raised α-fetoprotein, unlike non-seminomatous germ-cell tumours. A raised β-HCG never occurs in a normal male and is diagnostic of malignancy. After diagnosis of testicular cancer, a staging CT scan is required to assess the extent of disease and provide a baseline for response to treatment.

CT-guided biopsy of the chest lesion
CT-guided biopsy of the chest lesion is incorrect. CT-guided biopsy of the chest lesion is not necessary as the tissue diagnosis will be made at orchidectomy.

Orchidectomy
Orchidectomy is incorrect. Orchidectomy will be performed, but is not the appropriate next stage, as completion of staging takes priority. Orchidectomy with chemotherapy is curative in 90% of cases.

Testicular biopsy
Testicular biopsy is incorrect. Testicular biopsy is contraindicated owing to the risk of seeding the malignancy to the skin.

Testicular ultrasound
Testicular ultrasound is incorrect. Testicular ultrasound is not likely to alter the patient’s management in this case and would be used in the case of an indeterminate testicular mass without raised tumour markers.

stem: A 67-year-old patient with non-small-cell lung cancer complains of difficulty breathing, coughing and swelling of his face, neck, upper body and arms. Superior vena cava syndrome is diagnosed. Which of the following treatments is most likely to be successful in giving early and lasting relief of symptoms?
explanation:
Radiotherapy
Superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS) is a collection of symptoms caused by the partial blockage of the vein that carries blood from the head, neck, chest and arms to the heart. Symptoms can include difficulty breathing, coughing and swelling of the face, neck, upper body and arms. In rare instances patients complain of hoarseness, chest pain, difficulty swallowing and coughing up blood. Physical signs of SVCS include swelling of the neck or chest veins, collection of fluid in the face or arms, and rapid breathing. In patients with SVCS secondary to non-small-cell carcinoma of the lung, radiotherapy is the primary treatment of choice. The likelihood of patients benefiting from such therapy is high, but the overall prognosis of these patients is poor. The fractionation schedule for radiotherapy usually includes two to four large initial fractions of 3–4 Gy, followed by daily delivery of conventional fractions of 1.5–2 Gy, up to a total dose of 30–50 Gy. The radiation dose depends on tumour size and radioresponsiveness. The radiation field should include a 2 cm margin around the tumour.

Anti-hypertensive drugs
Anti-hypertensive drugs is incorrect. Anti-hypertensive therapy will have no influence on the underlying cause of SVCS and is not a key part of immediate management.

Chemotherapy
Chemotherapy is incorrect. NSCLC is a characteristically radio-sensitive and chemo-insensitive tumour and hence, chemotherapy is very unlikely to yield any benefit with the acute presentation of SVCS.

Corticosteroids
Corticosteroids is incorrect. Corticosteroids and diuretics are often used to relieve laryngeal or cerebral oedema related to SVCS, although documentation of their efficacy is questionable. Radiotherapy is the most likely of the options given to be successful in giving early relief of symptoms.

Surgical bypass
Surgical bypass is incorrect. Surgery for SVCS (surgical bypass) is rarely performed and is generally reserved for patients with advanced intrathoracic disease who have not responded to non-surgical treatments such as radiotherapy, chemotherapy and stenting.

stem: A 60-year-old woman, who has been a life-long smoker, has been recently diagnosed with lung cancer. Her husband asks you about how her smoking is likely to have contributed to her chances of developing this condition. Which one of the following best describes the contribution of smoking history to lung cancer risk?
options: Life-long smokers are particularly likely to develop adenocarcinoma compared with life-long nonsmokers
Life-long smokers have a 50% increased risk of developing cancer compared with non-smokers
Life-long smokers have a lung cancer risk 2–3 times greater than that of non-smokers
Non-smokers are more likely to develop small-cell cancers
The relative risk for developing small-cell lung cancer and squamous-cell lung cancer is increased in
explanation:
The relative risk for developing small-cell lung cancer and squamous-cell lung cancer is increased in
The relative risk for developing small-cell lung cancer and squamous-cell lung cancer is increased in smokers Lung cancer is the most common cancer in the world. The relative risk is greater for squamous-cell and smallcell lung cancers than for adenocarcinomas. In non-smokers with lung cancer, adenocarcinoma is the most frequently observed histological type.

Life-long smokers are particularly likely to develop adenocarcinoma compared with life-long nonsmokers
Life-long smokers are particularly likely to develop adenocarcinoma compared with life-long non-smokers is incorrect. The relative risk is greater for squamous-cell and small-cell lung cancers than for adenocarcinomas.

Life-long smokers have a 50% increased risk of developing cancer compared with non-smokers
Life-long smokers have a 50% increased risk of developing cancer compared with non-smokers is incorrect. The relative risk is 2000–3000% greater.

Life-long smokers have a lung cancer risk 2–3 times greater than that of non-smokers
Life-long smokers have a lung cancer risk 2–3 times greater than that of non-smokers is incorrect. Life-long smokers have a lung-cancer risk 20–30 times greater than that of a non-smoker.

Non-smokers are more likely to develop small-cell cancers
Non-smokers are more likely to develop small-cell cancers is incorrect. Smoking increases the risk of all histological types of lung cancers including small-cell lung cancer.

stem: A 60-year-old man presents with pain in his right flank and haematuria. A CT scan of the abdomen reveals a large 8 × 8-cm solid mass in the right kidney and a 3 × 3-cm solid mass occupying the upper pole of the left kidney. Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
options: Right radical nephrectomy and biopsy of the mass on the left side
Right radical nephrectomy and left partial nephrectomy
Right radical nephrectomy followed by interleukin-2
explanation:
Right radical nephrectomy and left partial nephrectomy
The classic triad of haematuria, loin pain and mass in the flank is suggestive of renal carcinoma. Since both kidneys are involved, a partial nephrectomy of the less-involved kidney is justified to preserve some renal function.

Bilateral nephrectomy
Bilateral nephrectomy is incorrect. Bilateral nephrectomy would be less desirable as there would be complete loss of renal function and also in this case, because one kidney is less involved than the other.

Interleukin-2 and interferon-α
Interleukin-2 and interferon-α is incorrect. Treatment with interleukin-2 and interferon alpha produces a remission in about 20% of cases. It is frequently used in addition to debulking surgery with promising results, rather than being used on its own. There are many new cytokine treatments recommended by NICE technology appraisal guidance (TA215 and TA169) for treatment of advanced and metastatic renal cell carcinoma, such as pazopanib and sunitinib.

Right radical nephrectomy and biopsy of the mass on the left side
Right radical nephrectomy and biopsy of the mass on the left side is incorrect. Right radical nephrectomy and biopsy of the mass on the left side would be incorrect as the left upper pole is likely to be carcinoma.

Right radical nephrectomy followed by interleukin-2.

stem: A 75-year-old retired car mechanic who is a smoker is diagnosed with lung cancer. Some 10 years ago he was treated with surgery and adjuvant chemotherapy for bladder cancer. His brother had oesophageal cancer aged 66 and another brother had prostate cancer in his 70s. His 55-year-old daughter was recently diagnosed with breast cancer. Which one of the following is the most likely explanation for the cancers in your patient?
options: The second tumour is a late complication of chemotherapy
explanation:
Exposure to tobacco smoke
It is not uncommon for an individual to have two different malignancies over a lifetime and sometimes this can be owing to a genetic predisposition, eg colorectal and endometrial cancer in a woman with hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer. There is a family history of cancer here, but they are all common cancers with no specific pattern or diagnosis at an early age. Features in a family history that would suggest a genetic predisposition include a young age at onset (typically below 50), specific combinations (eg breast and ovarian cancer), unusual cancers and multiple affected relatives. The carcinogen most likely to be implicated in both cancers in this case is tobacco smoke.

A hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome
There are no features suggesting a genetic predisposition here.

Exposure to aniline dyes
Aniline dye exposure is a risk factor for bladder cancer but there is no known association with lung cancer.

Exposure to asbestos
Asbestos exposure is a risk factor for mesothelioma but only rarely is associated with bladder cancer.

The second tumour is a late complication of chemotherapy
Lung cancer is not a common late complication of chemotherapy, and would be unlikely to develop within ten years of treatment for bladder cancer.

stem: A 37-year-old man previously fit and well man presents with hip pain and is diagnosed with a soft tissue sarcoma. He is found to have metastases in the lungs and bones. He is prescribed ifosfamide as part of a palliative multi-agent chemotherapy regime. Why was he also prescribed MESNA (2-mercaptoethane sulfonate Na)?
explanation:
To prevent haemorrhagic cystitis
MESNA is sodium 2-mercapto-ethanesulfonate. MESNA is a compound designed to function as a regional detoxificant of urotoxic chemotherapeutic agents such as ifosfamide and cyclophosphamide. After absorption MESNA is oxidised to MESNA disulfide; in the kidney it is reduced to MESNA, the free thiol compound, and this then binds to 4-hydroxy-ifosfamide, forming a non-urotoxic 4-sulfoethylthioifosfamide. Patients are advised to keep well hydrated following chemotherapy and to pass urine as soon as the urge is felt to minimise exposure of the bladder epithelium to cytotoxic agents.

To prevent alopecia
To prevent alopecia is incorrect. The use of a cold-cap is used to reduce chemotherapy-induced alopecia.

To prevent hepatic fibrosis
To prevent hepatic fibrosis is incorrect. Methotrexate not ifosfamide is associated with hepatic fibrosis.

To prevent mucositis
To prevent mucositis is incorrect. Oral care protocols exist for the management of chemotherapy-induced mucositis.

To prevent pulmonary fibrosis
To prevent pulmonary fibrosis is incorrect. Methotrexate not ifosfamide is associated with pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with diarrhoea. She explains she has a tumour but cannot remember the name of it. However, she is sure it has been described as ‘serotonin secreting’. What malignancy is she most likely to be suffering from?
explanation:
Neuroendocrine tumour of the ileum
Neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) are most commonly found in the ileum. Patients with these tumours have 5year survival rates in excess of 75%, in the absence of liver metastases. Multifocal small-bowel disease is present in approximately 30% of cases. NETs that are more than 2 cm in diameter have frequently metastasised when detected. Carcinoid syndrome due to excessive amounts of serotonin occurs in the presence of liver metastases. Treatment may involve resection of the primary tumour and hepatic metastases, the use of somatostatin analogues (octreotide) to control the effects of hormone excess, and peptide receptor radiotargeted therapy (PRRT).

Macrocystic pancreatic adenoma
Macrocystic pancreatic adenoma is incorrect. Macrocystic pancreatic adenomas are rare non-secretory tumours characterised by a multi-lobulated cystic lesion within the pancreas.

Mucinous pancreatic cystadenoma
Mucinous pancreatic cystadenoma is incorrect. Mucinous pancreatic cystadenomas are tumours of the mucinsecreting columnar epithelium within the pancreas and are usually solitary and benign.

Paraganglioma
Paraganglioma is incorrect. Most paragangliomas are tumours of the sympathetic nervous system originating in variable sites, including carotid body, glomus jugulare and sympathetic paravertebral ganglion of the abdomen, and rarely may secrete catecholamines (approximately 2% of tumours). Some parasympathetic paragangliomas are described, most often in the neck, and are non-secreting.

stem: A 36-year-old woman has been investigated for hypercalcaemia and is found to have hyperparathyroidism. There is a family history that makes an underlying diagnosis of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN 1) suspected. Which one of the following best fits with the clinical features of this condition?
options: It includes medullary-cell carcinoma of the thyroid
It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
Patients have a normal life expectancy
explanation:
Primary hyperparathyroidism is common
Multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) is an autosomal dominant disorder characterised by a high frequency of peptic ulcer disease (Zollinger–Ellison syndrome) and primary endocrine abnormalities involving the pituitary, parathyroid and pancreas. Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common abnormality. Patients have a decreased life expectancy, with a 50% probability of death by the age of 50 years.

It includes medullary-cell carcinoma of the thyroid
It includes medullary-cell carcinoma of the thyroid is incorrect. Medullary-cell carcinoma occurs in MEN 2a and MEN 2b.

It includes phaeochromocytoma
It includes phaeochromocytoma is incorrect. Phaeochromocytomas occur in MEN 2a and MEN 2b.

It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner
It is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner is incorrect. MEN is an autosomal dominant disorder.

Patients have a normal life expectancy
Patients have a normal life expectancy is incorrect. Patients have a decreased life expectancy, with a 50% probability of death by the age of 50 years. Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia You are asked to review an 86-year-old patient on the ward who is complaining of abdominal pain. Upon review of his notes, you learn he has colon cancer and he has been admitted for severe constipation. He had been improving in the last few days, but he is still struggling with abdominal pain, mainly in the left iliac fossa. His current medications include senna, metformin, bisoprolol, clopidogrel and omeprazole. On examination, the abdomen is soft, but there is generalised discomfort on palpation, especially in the left iliac fossa. An abdominal X-ray shows faecal loading.

stem: An 80-year-old man presented with symptoms of nocturia and decreased urinary flow. Benign prostatic hypertrophy was diagnosed and he was prescribed an α-blocker. He now presents, 2 years later, with back pain. Prostatic carcinoma with metastases is diagnosed. Which of the following best describes the percentage of men aged 80 who have malignant foci within their prostate gland?
explanation:
80%
Prostatic carcinoma accounts for 7% of all male cancers and is the fourth commonest cause of death from malignant disease in men. By 80 years of age some 80% of men appear to have malignant foci within the prostate gland. Some commentators have suggested screening for cases with prostate-specific antigen (PSA), but this has not yet been proposed for the UK. These are adenocarcinomas, and hormonal factors are thought to play a part in the aetiology. Presentation may be with symptoms of urinary tract obstruction, or later with symptoms of metastatic disease. According to the NICE guidelines (CG175), ‘if the clinical suspicion of prostate cancer is high, because of a high PSA and evidence of bone metastases (from positive isotope bone scan or sclerotic metastases on plain radiographs) then do not offer prostate biopsy for histological confirmation, unless it is required as part of a clinical trial’. Treatment depends on histological grading of the tumour and whether there is extracapsular spread. For younger patients with little comorbidity, surgical prostatectomy may be considered but radiotherapy is the suitable choice for many patients. Metastatic disease is managed with luteinising hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues. The value of non-hormonal chemotherapy is unproven.

30%
30% is incorrect. Prostate cancer is predominantly a disease in males over 65, however around 25% of cases occur in men under 65.

40%
40% is incorrect. Incidence of prostate cancer increase with age, with the highest incidence in those aged 90 or over.

45%
45% is incorrect. Prostate cancer is more common in black males than in white males, and least common in Asian males.

50%
50% is incorrect. More than half of prostate cancer cases in the UK each year are diagnosed in males aged 70 or over.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presented with abdominal distension and malaise. She was found to have a malignant ovarian carcinoma which had metastasised to the peritoneum and was causing ascites. She will receive combination chemotherapy with cisplatin as part of her treatment for advanced ovarian carcinoma. Which one of the following correctly describes the mode of action of cisplatin?
options: It is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor
It is a small molecule kinase inhibitor
It leads to cross-linking of DNA to form adducts
explanation:
It leads to cross-linking of DNA to form adducts
The mode of action of cisplatin is to promote cross-linking of DNA to form DNA adducts. This leads to promotion of intracellular signalling via pathways such as p53, p73 and MAP kinase leading to increased cellular apoptosis. Resistance to cisplatin may occur because of reduced cisplatin uptake by resistant cells or increased DNA adduct repair. Other mechanisms include loss of the p53-mediated pathway for programmed cell death. Side-effects include nephrotoxicity, neurotoxicity, ototoxicity and particularly electrolyte disturbance, including hypomagnesaemia, hypokalaemia and hypocalcaemia.

It inhibits protein synthesis
It inhibits protein synthesis is incorrect. Inhibition of protein synthesis describes the mechanism of action of a group of cytotoxics known as antimetabolites, e.g. fluorouracil, which inhibit the synthesis of nucleic acids.

It is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor
It is an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor is incorrect. Inhibition of epidermal growth factor receptor describes monoclonal antibodies such as cetuximab which target the epidermal growth factor receptor and are utilised when molecular testing demonstrates amplification of this receptor on the malignant cells.

It is a small molecule kinase inhibitor
It is a small molecule kinase inhibitor is incorrect. Inhibition of small molecule kinase describes molecularly targeted agents such as imatinib and sunitinib, which inhibit tyrosine kinases that are pathologically stimulated in malignant cells.

It is a topoisomerase inhibitor
It is a topoisomerase inhibitor is incorrect. Inhibition of topoisomerase describes one of the mechanisms of action of anthracycline agents such as doxorubicin, which inhibit the topoisomerase enzymes critical to DNA replication and transcription.

stem: A 49-year-old man presents with weight loss and is found to have a 5 cm tumour abutting the wall of the stomach. Upon resection it is found to be a gastrointestinal stromal tumour. He is referred to you for consideration of adjuvant therapy. You decide to prescribe him long-term imatinib therapy. What is the mode of action of imatinib?
options: Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitor
explanation:
Tyrosine kinase inhibitor
Imatinib was originally developed for the treatment of chronic myeloid leukaemia, and is specific for the tyrosine kinases coded for by the bcr-abl translocation (c-kit) and tyrosine kinase activity related to the platelet-derived growth factor receptor. It is also utilised in the management of gastrointestinal stromal tumours, which are driven by the same fusion gene. Common side-effects include oedema, rash, nausea and musculoskeletal pain, but patients normally report these as mild. Severe congestive cardiac failure is a rare side-effect of therapy.

Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor
Epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor is incorrect. An example of an epidermal growth factor receptor inhibitor is cetuximab, a monoclonal antibody utilised in the management of colorectal cancer.

Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor
Dihydrofolate reductase inhibitor is incorrect. An example of a folic acid antagonist is methotrexate, which inhibits dihydrofolate reductase as its mechanism of action.

Serine kinase inhibitor
Serine kinase inhibitor is incorrect. Serine kinase inhibitors are not currently in routine clinical use but in development in clinical trials.

Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitor
Vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitor is incorrect. An example of a vascular endothelial growth factor receptor inhibitor is sunitinib, which is utilised in the management of renal cell carcinoma.

stem: The advent of targeted anti-cancer therapies has revolutionised treatment of many malignancies. Following the paradigm of personalised medicine, molecular testing of tumours is now routine in order to identify specific genetic alterations predictive of response to particular therapies. Which of the following neoplasms most frequently responds to specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors?
explanation:
Gastrointestinal stromal tumours
Specific tyrosine kinase inhibitors were developed after it was recognised that the Philadelphia chromosome (translocation 9:22) was associated with bcr-abl tyrosine kinase overexpression. STI571, later known as imatinib mesylate (Gleevec), was therefore designed to treat chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML), but it was also found to be effective in gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GIST) – previously known as leiomyosarcoma. The high prevalence of the brc-abl translocation in GIST and CML (approximately 90%) means that management has been revolutionised by the introduction of targeted therapies such as imatinib.

Acute lymphocytic leukaemia
Acute lymphocytic leukaemia is incorrect. Acute lymphocytic leukaemia may be suitable for treatment with targeted therapies but not in such large proportions.

Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia is incorrect. Acute myeloid leukaemia may be suitable for treatment with targeted therapies but not in such large proportions.

Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia
Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia is incorrect. Chronic lymphocytic leukaemia may be suitable for treatment with targeted therapies but not in such large proportions.

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. Multiple myeloma may be suitable for treatment with targeted therapies but not in such large proportions.

stem: A 45-year-old male smoker presents with a short history over the last few weeks of haemoptysis and increasing shortness of breath. A chest X-ray shows a right hilar mass. He is admitted to hospital for diagnostic investigations and staging. These reveal the presence of hepatic lesions. During his admission, he develops a left hemiparesis. Which one of the following is the most likely histological diagnosis?
explanation:
Small-cell lung carcinoma
Small-cell lung cancer is the most likely diagnosis. This is an aggressive cancer which typically presents with a short history and 80–90% will have metastases at the time of presentation. In this patient, the liver lesions are likely to represent metastases and his development of left-sided weakness suggests the likely presence of cerebral metastases. Cytotoxic chemotherapy with a platinum-based regimen would be the treatment of choice.
