Initially small-cell lung cancer is chemosensitive and an improvement may be expected; however, this is usually short-lived and the median survival is 6–12 months.

Adenocarcinoma of the lung
Adenocarcinoma of the lung is incorrect. Owing to a longer natural history this pathological subtype of lung cancer is less likely.

Large-cell lung carcinoma
Large-cell lung carcinoma is incorrect. Owing to a longer natural history this pathological subtype of lung cancer is less likely.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect. However, this diagnosis would need to be excluded as lymphoma is potentially curable. The smoking history and respiratory symptoms make lung cancer more likely.

Squamous-cell lung carcinoma
Squamous-cell lung carcinoma is incorrect. Owing to a longer natural history this pathological subtype of lung cancer is less likely.

stem: A patient diagnosed with carcinoma of the colon underwent a hemicolectomy. Staging is T3, N1, M0. Based on large clinical trials, which treatment is most likely to this patient’s overall survival?
options: Postoperative radiotherapy and chemotherapy with doxorubicin
explanation:
Chemotherapy with 5-fluorouracil and folinic acid
This patient has Dukes’ C carcinoma of the colon. The Dukes’ classification of colorectal carcinomas remains the mainstay of tumour staging: Stage A disease is confined to the bowel wall with no extension to the serosal fat. Stage B disease involves the full thickness of the bowel wall with extension through to the serosa. Stage C involves the spread of tumour to draining lymph nodes. Stage D disease involves distant spread, primarily to the liver. 5-Fluorouracil (5-FU) (with folinic acid) prolongs the survival of patients with stage D disease. Randomised trials have also shown that 5-FU improves survival in stage C disease when used as adjuvant therapy to surgery. The evidence of survival advantage from adjuvant chemotherapy in stage B disease is less clear.

High-dose multivitamins
High-dose multivitamins is incorrect. There is no role for high-dose multivitamins in cancer management.

Low-fat diet
Low-fat diet is incorrect. Low-fat diet is known to reduce the incidence of colorectal cancer but has not been proven to outcomes once malignancy has been diagnosed.

Postoperative radiotherapy
Postoperative radiotherapy is incorrect. Post- (and pre-) operative radiotherapy is used primarily in cancers of the rectum and anus where significant survival benefits have been proven, but is not utilised in the routine management of colon cancer.

Postoperative radiotherapy and chemotherapy with doxorubicin
Postoperative radiotherapy and chemotherapy with doxorubicin is incorrect. Post- (and pre-) operative radiotherapy is used primarily in cancers of the rectum and anus where significant survival benefits have been proven, but is not utilised in the routine management of colon cancer.

stem: A 64-year-old man is seen in the Outpatient Department with a persistent cough. He is a heavy smoker and has a history of diverticulitis. On examination, he is clubbed, is hyperresonant throughout his chest and has a bilateral expiratory wheeze with oxygen saturations of 92%. He has an ejection systolic murmur at the aortic area. His abdomen is slightly tender in the left iliac fossa. FBC shows Hb 142 g/l, WCC 28 × 10 3/mm 3 (neutrophils 24 × 10 3/mm 3, lymphocytes 3.3 × 10 3/mm 3), platelets 198 × 10 3/mm 3. His CRP is measured at 12. His temperature is 36.8°C. Which one of the following is the likely cause of the neutrophilia?
explanation:
Paraneoplastic neutrophilia
This man is a heavy smoker who is clubbed with a raised white cell count. He is afebrile. He has a persistent cough, suggesting underlying lung carcinoma. Putting all of this together, the idea of a leukemoid reaction, also known as a paraneoplastic neutrophilia, is the correct answer.

Acute myeloid leukaemia
Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is incorrect, because this is a predominant neutrophilia with no suggestion of blast cells. The patient is not anaemic or thrombocytopenic, which would be expected in AML.

Diverticulitis
Diverticulitis is incorrect because the man is afebrile with a low CRP. This diagnosis has nothing to do with all the other more pertinent information given in the question.

Pneumonia
Pneumonia is incorrect because, again, he is afebrile with a low CRP and there is more pertinent information to suggest underlying malignancy with a resultant leukemoid reaction.

Endocarditis
Endocarditis is incorrect–again this is false because of the low CRP level, the fact that he is afebrile and the other more pertinent information in the question.

stem: A 75-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with frank haematuria. His past medical history includes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and osteoarthritis. He is a retired bus driver and an ex-smoker with a 20-pack-year history. Other than his inhalers, he does not take any other medications. After 24 hours of bladder irrigation, the bleeding stops, and the patient is discharged with a view to performing a cystoscopy as an outpatient. This shows a solitary exophytic mass arising from the bladder wall that has a diameter of 2 cm. A staging computed tomography (CT) is performed, which does not show significant lymphadenopathy or metastases. Cytological analysis suggests a papillary urothelial neoplasm. Which of the following would be the correct management?
options: Perform a radical cystectomy, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy
Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) and offer a single dose of
Offer neo-adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin, followed by radical cystectomy or radical
Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), followed by instillation of
explanation:
Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) and offer a single dose of
Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT) and offer a single dose of intravesical mitomycin C This man has bladder cancer. The treatment decision is based on risk stratification, patient’s decision and performance status. In absence of muscle invasion, lymphadenopathy, metastases and aggressive histological types, this case constitutes a low-risk non-invasive bladder neoplasm. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, TURBT with one of photodynamic diagnosis, narrow-band imaging, cytology or a urinary biomarker, constitutesChat the with best management option in this case. The procedure should include a biopsy of detrusor muscle for histological analysis. A single dose of mytomicin C should be offered during the same session. A further TURBT should be carried out in six weeks if no detrusor muscle biopsy was undertaken. It is recommended that patients undergo cystoscopic follow-up three months and 12 months after diagnosis. Patients who have had low-risk non-muscle-invasive bladder cancer and who have no recurrence of the bladder cancer within 12 months should be discharged to primary care.

Perform a radical cystectomy, followed by adjuvant chemotherapy
Adjuvant cisplatin combination chemotherapy after radical cystectomy should be considered for people with a diagnosis of muscle-invasive or lymph-node-positive urothelial bladder cancer and for whom neoadjuvant chemotherapy is not suitable.

Offer neo-adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin, followed by radical cystectomy or radical
Offer neo-adjuvant chemotherapy with cisplatin, followed by radical cystectomy or radical radiotherapy Neoadjuvant chemotherapy using a cisplatin combination regimen before radical cystectomy or radical radiotherapy is the treatment of choice for people with newly diagnosed muscle-invasive urothelial bladder cancer.

Instillation of Bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG)
The choice of intravesical BCG or radical cystectomy should be given to patients with high-risk non-muscleinvasive bladder cancer. BCG is a form of immunotherapy that exploits a tuberculosis vaccine developed from Mycobacterium bovis. Its exact mechanism of action in bladder tumours remains unclear, but it is thought to revolve around local immune cell activation with inflammatory response, direct cancer cell infection and induction of antitumour effects.

Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), followed by instillation of
Proceed with transurethral resection of bladder tumour (TURBT), followed by instillation of intravesical BCG The choice of intravesical BCG or radical cystectomy should be given to patients with high-risk non-muscleinvasive bladder cancer.

stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to the Oncology Clinic for assessment. She presented to her GP some 3 weeks earlier with unsteadiness on her feet and a lump in her left breast. She has been diagnosed with a cancer in the left breast, and has significant cerebellar symptoms with diplopia, dysarthria and ataxia. MRI of the brain is unremarkable. Which of the following autoantibodies are most likely to be found?
explanation:
Anti-Yo
Anti-Yo antibodies primarily occur in patients with paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD) who have breast cancer or tumours of the ovary, endometrium and fallopian tube. PCD is thought to be triggered when tumour cells express proteins normally expressed in the cerebellum, triggering an autoimmune reaction. Symptoms may include dysarthria, ataxia and nystagmus. Neurological outcome is generally poor; although removal of the primary tumour leads to stabilisation of symptoms, improvement is very rarely seen.

Anti-Hu
Anti-Hu is incorrect. Anti-Hu antibodies are associated with underlying small-cell cancer.

Anti-Ro
Anti-Ro is incorrect. Anti-Ro antibodies are associated with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and neonatal heart block.

Anti-Tr
Anti-Tr is incorrect. Anti-Tr antibodies are associated with Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Anti-Zic4
Anti-Zic4 is incorrect. Anti-Zic4 antibodies are associated with small-cell lung cancer.

stem: The headmaster of the local school had recently been diagnosed as having prostatic carcinoma. Lately he had suffered bone pain, was anaemic and had striking changes on the blood film. Which one of the following is the most likely blood-film abnormality?
explanation:
Leukoerythroblastic blood film
Leucoerythroblastic blood film is the most likely blood film abnormality. We are told that this man has bone pain in the setting of prostatic carcinoma, so this suggests that metastatic disease has spread to the bone. We are told that this man is anaemic, and has striking changes on the blood film. This is therefore most likely of bone marrow spread by the prostate cancer, which will result in a leucoerythroblastic blood picture. This is characterised by the presence of immature white and red blood cells on the peripheral blood film.

Anaemia on blood film
Anaemia on blood film is incorrect. Anaemia on the blood film is difficult to spot. Anaemia is not a change that can be described on a blood film accurately.

Leukaemoid reaction on blood film
Leukaemoid reaction on blood film is incorrect. Patients with malignant disease can have a high white cell count as a result of what is known as a leukaemoid reaction. However, this would not necessarily fit in with the fact that he has bone pain, and the fact that he is anaemic.

Microangiopathic blood film
Microangiopathic blood film is incorrect. Microangiopathic blood film can be found in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP). This can be an association with malignant disease. We are not told that this man has a low platelet count or any symptoms of thrombocytopenia. We are told, however, that this man has bone pain, which suggests metastatic bony disease, and therefore bone marrow invasion resulting in a leucoerythroblastic blood picture would be much more likely.

Thrombocytopenia on blood film
Thrombocytopenia on blood film is incorrect. Thrombocytopenia on a blood film really is not a striking change on the blood film. Again, for the above reasons, leucoerythroblastic blood film would be more likely.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to his GP with an enlarging skin lesion affecting his lower lip. He first noticed it approximately 6 months ago and he complains of occasional bleeding and itching from the lesion. A dermatology referral is made and, after excision biopsy, a squamous-cell carcinoma of his lower lip is diagnosed. Which one of the following is most likely to be a feature of this type of carcinoma?
options: It commonly spreads to distant sites by venous channels
It is capable of metastasising via the lymphatics
It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age
It most commonly arises on the torso
Survival is measured in weeks to months
explanation:
It is capable of metastasising via the lymphatics
Squamous-cell carcinoma of the skin is the second most common skin cancer in the UK and is related to sun exposure. A squamous-cell carcinoma usually appears as a scaly or crusty area of skin, with a red, inflamed base. Most small squamous-cell carcinomas are not painful. Squamous-cell carcinoma of the skin is seldom seen in persons under 45 years of age. It is related to UV exposure and usually occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the face and lower lips. Squamous-cell carcinomas may arise from areas of Bowen’s disease and sometimes in the margin of a chronic leg ulcer. Excision biopsy is essential for accurate diagnosis. Chronic immunosuppression is also a risk factor and they are relatively more common in patients who have received an organ transplant. Radical surgery and radiotherapy are the treatment of choice. It spreads to distant sites by the lymphatic channels not venous channels.

It commonly spreads to distant sites by venous channels
It commonly spreads to distant sites by venous channels is incorrect. It spreads to distant sites by the lymphatic channels, not venous channels.

It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age
It is commonly seen in patients under 45 years of age is incorrect. Squamous-cell carcinoma of the skin is seldom seen in persons under 45 years of age.

It most commonly arises on the torso
It most commonly arises on the torso is incorrect. Squamous-cell carcinoma of the skin is related to UV exposure and usually occurs in sun-exposed areas such as the face and lower lips.

Survival is measured in weeks to months
Survival is measured in weeks to months is incorrect, even advanced SCCs can usually be excised, and distant spread with the consequences of metastasis is rare.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a six-month history of fatigue, night sweats and unintentional weight loss. On examination, he has non-tender lymphadenopathy in the cervical and supraclavicular regions. A subsequent biopsy confirms a diagnosis of Hodgkin's lymphoma. What is the most appropriate first-line treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy
The standard first-line treatment for Hodgkin's lymphoma typically involves a combination of chemotherapy and radiotherapy, especially in patients with early-stage disease (stages I or II). This approach maximises the chances of remission by targeting both localised tumours with radiation while addressing potential systemic spread using chemotherapy. Regimens such as ABVD (adriamycin, bleomycin, vinblastine, dacarbazine) are commonly used, followed by involved-site radiation therapy to achieve optimal outcomes.

Chemotherapy alone
While chemotherapy is an essential component of Hodgkin's lymphoma treatment, it is often combined with radiotherapy to efficacy in many cases. Sole reliance on chemotherapy may be reserved for advanced stages or specific clinical scenarios.

Radiotherapy alone
Radiotherapy can effectively target localised lymph node involvement; however, it does not address systemic disease which could be present even if not detected initially. Using radiotherapy as monotherapy might lead to incomplete eradication of cancer cells outside the irradiated field.

Stem cell transplant
Stem cell transplantation after high-dose chemotherapy is generally reserved for relapsed or refractory cases where initial treatments have failed. It is not considered a first-line option due to its intensity and associated risks compared to initial combined modality treatments.

Surgery
Surgical intervention plays a limited role in treating Hodgkin's lymphoma because this type of cancer typically spreads through lymphatic pathways rather than forming isolated masses that can be surgically removed. Surgery may be used primarily for diagnostic purposes rather than therapeutic management. Hodgkin’s.

stem: A 40-year-old Indian man presents with night sweats, loin pain, haematuria and proteinuria. He has a past medical history of recurrent urinary tract infections. On examination a left-sided varicocele is noted. His serum calcium level is raised and haemoglobin is low. Which one of the following is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Hypernephroma
Hypernephroma (clear cell or renal adenocarcinoma) affects men twice as often as women in 40–60-year-olds. Haematogenous spread to bone causes lytic lesions and hypercalcaemia. A classic triad of haematuria, loin pain and abdominal mass is usually noted. Other manifestations are night sweats and a left varicocele due to compression of the left renal vein. None of these conditions (other than hypernephroma) would have a left varicocele as a characteristic finding.

Chronic pyelonephritis
Chronic pyelonephritis is incorrect. Chronic pyelonephritis due to recurrent bacterial infections would not usually present with haematuria alone; serum calcium would also not be elevated. It is characterised by renal inflammation and fibrosis caused by recurrent urinary infection, urinary tract obstruction or vesicoureteral reflux. The diagnosis may be based on ultrasound or CT scanning.

Henoch–Schönlein purpura
Henoch–Schönlein purpura is incorrect. Henoch–Schönlein purpura would present with a purpuric rash over the buttocks and extensor surfaces. In addition, there may be arthralgia and abdominal pain that can develop before the rash appears. It affects patients of any age, but the majority of cases occur in children under 10 years of age.

Renal tuberculosis
Renal tuberculosis is incorrect. Renal tuberculosis may present with night sweats and haematuria, but hypercalcaemia is not a typical feature. Tuberculosis of the kidney results from haematogenous seeding of Mycobacterium tuberculosis in the glomerular and peritubular capillary beds from the lungs. Other symptoms may include frequency of urination and abdominal pain. There is often a long latency period (5–40 years) between initial infection and renal tuberculosis. To investigate, three first-morning midstream urine should be cultured for acid-fast bacilli.

Renal vein thrombosis
Renal vein thrombosis is incorrect. A left varicocele may also occur with left renal vein thrombosis, but night sweats, haematuria and hypercalcaemia are not seen. There may be numerous aetiologies for renal vein thrombosis; however, it occurs most frequently in patients with nephrotic syndrome. Over the past two weeks, he has had little food or fluids as they get ‘stuck’ and are painful to swallow. His regular medications include domperidone, omeprazole, aspirin and bisoprolol; however, he has not been able to take them due to his symptoms. Two weeks ago, he received a course of radiotherapy to reduce the size of the primary lesion, whereas the last cycle of chemotherapy was completed a month ago. On examination, you notice radiotherapy marks with surrounding skin redness on the patient’s chest. Investigations.

stem: Which of the following is the investigation most likely to elucidate the cause of his blood picture?
explanation:
Incubate serum at 4 °C
The most likely cause of this man’s anaemia, acrocyanosis and Raynaud’s is cryoglobulinaemia as a result of underlying lymphoma. As such, when serum is incubated at 4 °C, cryoglobulins are seen to precipitate. Typing of the lymphoma is crucial with respect to determining management, and as such, lymph node excision to confirm the diagnosis is an obvious next step.

Bone marrow aspiration
Bone marrow aspiration is incorrect. Bone marrow aspiration is an ideal investigation to diagnose lymphoproliferative disorders. In the presence of normal white cell count and platelet counts, as well as acute symptoms, this is unlikely, even with lymphadenopathy.

Check C3 and C4 levels
Check C3 and C4 levels is incorrect. C3 and C4 would levels are measured if active lupus is suspected.

Check mycoplasma serology
Check mycoplasma serology is incorrect. Mycoplasma serology is useful in diagnosing Mycoplasma pneumonia infections in the chest. On infection, patients first develop headache, malaise and fever. This is followed by an intractable, non-productive cough, which only progresses to pneumonia in a minority of patients. This may be associated with pleural effusion but chest signs may be absent. The absence of these symptoms makes this diagnosis less likely and the chronic nature of his symptoms, coupled with lymphadenopathy makes a haematological malignancy much more likely.

Osmotic fragility test
Osmotic fragility test is incorrect. Osmotic fragility testing is performed to confirm a diagnosis of hereditary spherocytosis. Hereditary spherocytosis is a common cause of haemolytic anaemia due to defect in the red cell membrane. Presentation can be with anaemia, jaundice and splenomegaly. It can also be associated with gallstones. Osmotic fragility is diagnostic. The presence of lymphadenopathy suggests an alternative diagnosis, as does the high ESR. Non-Hodgkin’s Lymphoma A 65-year-old hospice-resident with metastatic breast cancer presents with a 24-hour history of bilateral leg weakness and severe lower back pain. Her background includes ischaemic heart disease, type II diabetes and fibromyalgia. She has had one episode of urinary incontinence on her way to the hospital. On examination, she showed decreased power on both legs and reduced anal tone. There is mid-spine tenderness on palpation of her lower spine.

stem: Serum tumour markers are frequently utilised in the management of cancer patients. The determination of the carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) in patients with carcinoma of the colon is most useful for which one of the following?
options: The detection of an early stage tumour
explanation:
For postoperative surveillance
CEA is an oncofetal protein that is elevated in the serum of patients with a variety of cancers, including colorectal cancer. In patients with established disease, the absolute level of the serum CEA correlates with disease burden and should return to baseline after complete resection. Between 60 and 90% of patients with a relapse have elevated CEA (ref Hara M, Kanemitsu Y, Hirai T, Dis. Colon Rectum, 2008).

As a parameter for operability
As a parameter for operability is incorrect. Serum CEA has no bearing as a parameter for operability.

As a screening method
As a screening method is incorrect. Because it lacks both sensitivity and specificity, serum CEA is not a useful screening tool for colorectal cancer. Non-cancer-related causes of an elevated CEA include gastritis, peptic ulcer disease, diverticulitis and liver disease. Colorectal cancer screening involves faecal occult blood testing and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy.

For staging
For staging is incorrect. Tumour staging does not include CEA levels and is based on tumour, node, metastasis (TNM) histopathological evaluation. Pre-surgical staging evaluations include CT imaging of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis, MRI of the rectum in the case of rectal tumours, and PET scanning in the case of uncertainty over presence of metastatic disease.

The detection of an early stage tumour
The detection of an early stage tumour is incorrect. Serum CEA lacks sensitivity and specificity and so is not a useful diagnostic tool for detection of early stage cancers.

stem: A 62-year-old woman presents with painless haematuria. She is a heavy smoker and has a history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She previously lived in Australia and has used substantial amounts of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for arthritis, particularly phenacetin some years ago. Renal function testing is unremarkable. She has a raised plasma viscosity and is anaemic, with a haemoglobin of 100 g/l (115–155 g/l). Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Squamous cell carcinoma of the kidney
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
explanation:
Transitional cell carcinoma of the bladder
Transitional cell tumours account for around 3% of deaths from malignancy. They are uncommon below the age of 40 years and have a male to female ratio of 4:1. Bladder tumours are 50 times more common than tumours of the ureter or renal pelvis. Predisposing factors include smoking; exposure to industrial carcinogens associated with the chemical and rubber industries; phenacetin and cyclophosphamide use; and chronic inflammation such as that caused by schistosomiasis (schistosomiasis is associated with squamous cell carcinoma). Presentation is commonly with painless haematuria, although pain may occur due to clot retention. According to NICE guidelines (NG2), it is important not to substitute urinary biomarkers for cystoscopy in the investigation of bladder cancer. CT and MRI staging should be considered before transurethral resection of bladder tumour if muscle-invasive bladder cancer is suspected at cystoscopy. The 5-year survival rate ranges from between 80 and 90% for small, early tumours to 5% when patients present with metastases.

Adenocarcinoma of the kidney
Adenocarcinoma of the kidney is incorrect. This would present with loin pain, haematuria and renal mass. It is also known as hypernephroma. There are several types: 75% are clear cell, 10% are papillary and 5% are chromophobe renal cell cancer. Rarer cancers include cancer of the collecting ducts and renal medullary carcinoma.

Nephrolithiasis
Nephrolithiasis is incorrect. This would present with renal colic and there is no associated anaemia, unlike in this case.

Squamous cell carcinoma of the kidney
Squamous cell carcinoma of the kidney is incorrect. This would present with loin pain, haematuria and renal mass. It is an extremely rare condition, constituting 0.5-15% of urothelial malignancies. Most patients are diagnosed at an advanced stage with poor outcome. Radical nephrectomy is the mainstay of treatment.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents with an erythematous facial rash, muscle pain and weakness in her shoulder and hips. She has been also complaining of lethargy, weight loss and persistent bloating for the past four months. She has no known past medical history. On examination, she has an erythematous swollen rash with scratch marks around her eyes, on her upper torso and proximally on her limbs. Erythema and oedema are also present symmetrically on her knuckles. She is also unable to lift her arms above her head. Which of the following would fit with the patient's presentation?
explanation:
Ovarian cancer
The rash features, which appears oedematous and symmetrical around eyes, upper torso, limbs and knuckles, associated with proximal weakness in a young woman suggests a diagnosis of dermatomyositis. It is important to remember that dermatomyositis can constitute the first presenting feature of various types of malignancies, including ovarian, breast, lung and pancreatic cancer. In up to one in ten patients with dermatomyositis, there is an underlying diagnosis of ovarian cancer. It is therefore important to carefully investigate patients with such a diagnosis in order to rule out hidden neoplasm. As the patient described in this scenario has persistent bloating, weight loss and lethargy preceding the rash and weakness, the most likely underlying diagnosis is ovarian cancer.

Systemic lupus erythematous (SLE)
SLE can present with various degrees and types of skin rashes: the classic 'butterfly rash' with redness across cheeks and nose, red, raised scaly non-scarring rash on sun-exposed areas or red to purple rash with discolouration and scarring. Meanwhile, the lesions described in this scenario (oedematous erythema involving eyes, upper torso, limbs and knuckles) with proximal muscle weakness are more suggestiveChat of with AI dermatomyositis. Tutor Ovarian, lung, pancreatic and breast cancer are all associated with dermatomyositis, which can be the first presenting feature. Because the patient is female and reports early weight loss and bloating, the most likely underlying disease is ovarian cancer.

Coeliac disease
One of the features of coeliac disease is dermatitis herpetiforme. Typical presentation includes red, raised patches, often with blister, causing severe itching. The classic distribution is on elbows, knees and buttocks. Coeliac disease can present with or without gastrointestinal symptoms and delayed presentation is more and more common, so that diagnosis is often made in adults. In this scenario, the proximal weakness, the distribution and features of the rash, would be more compatible with dermatomyositis. This can be associated with different types of malignancies and patients should be thoroughly investigated. In a woman with persistent bloating and new diagnosis of dermatomyositis, a gynaecological tumour should be suspected. Therefore, the correct answer is ovarian cancer.

Inclusion body myositis
Inclusion body myositis is a muscle inflammatory and degenerative condition, characterising by both abnormal protein accumulation and immune dysregulation. As a myopathic process, it normally presents with weakness with variable distribution, but in general both proximal and distal are affected. It is not associated with a rash. In this case, the flat symmetrical erythematous rash with oedema, coupled with proximal weakness, would not fit the clinical presentation of inclusion body myositis. Moreover, the red flag offered by the patient gender and abdominal symptoms prompt investigation for possible underlying ovarian cancer.

Systemic scleroderma (SS)
SS can affect both skin and organs. The typical skin manifestations include thickening of fingers and toes, sclerotic shiny skin lesions on limbs, abnormal nail, telangiectasis and microstomia. SS can be associated with myositis. In this case, the distribution and the features of the rash are more compatible with dermatomyositis, where the rash is usually flat, erythematous and oedematous, often around the eyes and involving knuckles. The proximal weakness is also characteristic. In a woman with abdominal symptoms and new diagnosis of dermatomyositis, it is important to rule out ovarian cancer, as this can present with dermatomyositis in up to 9% of the cases. The patient depicted complains of lethargy, weight loss and abdominal symptoms. Therefore, the most likely underlying issue among the options given is ovarian cancer. stem: Electrocardiogram (ECG) shows: sinus rhythm; PR interval 120 ms; normal QRS complexes; no ST depression/elevation; QTc: 510 ms; heart rate 95 bpm. What is the next most appropriate intervention?
options: Oesophageal-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) with a view of placing a stent
Naso-gastric tube insertion and artificial feeding
explanation:
Intravenous (IV) magnesium replacement
Radiotherapy is often part of the therapeutic schedule in the treatment of lung cancer – especially when this is advanced and not operable. This is often the case with small cell lung cancer. Patients can experience a variety of side-effects involving gastrointestinal, respiratory, urogenital or skin systems, depending on the areas treated. The description of gradual but sudden onset (two weeks’ history) of burning retrosternal chest pain and painful swallowing with additional evidence of dermatitis around radiotherapy marks strongly suggests that the cause of this patient’s symptoms is radiation oesophagitis. Treatment is conservative with topical gel lidocaine, high-dose proton pump inhibitors and pro-motility agents. Electrolytes abnormalities should be promptly corrected, and IV fluid replacement should be commenced, especially while patients are unable to eat or drink. In this case, there are multiple electrolytes abnormalities; however, the presence of a long QTc and low magnesium puts priority on IV magnesium replacement as the patient is at risk of developing cardiac arrhythmia.

Oesophageal-gastroduodenoscopy (OGD) with a view of placing a stent
This patient has recently received radiotherapy against a malignant lung mass. The symptoms described suggest that he has developed radiation oesophagitis, a common complication of radiotherapy. The treatment for this is conservative with IV electrolytes replacement, topical lidocaine, proton-pump inhibitors and pro-motility agents. Though oesophageal metastases can occur with lung cancer, the onset would have been more gradual and over a longer period. Therefore, an OGD with stenting is not indicated at this time.

IV potassium replacement
This patient has radiation oesophagitis and therefore has had low oral intake, resulting in multiple electrolytes abnormalities. Potassium and magnesium metabolisms are strictly linked, as a decrease in intracellular magnesium causes less inhibition of renal outer medullary potassium channel (ROMK) channels, resulting in higher potassium secretion in the distal nephrons. Hence, magnesium should be given in the first instance, in order to facilitate potassium replacement. In this case, the presence of hypomagnesaemia-induced long QTc also puts priority on magnesium replacement, due to risk of cardiac arrhythmia.

IV 0.9% saline
The symptoms described (gradual and rapid onset odynophagia and dysphagia) and the skin rash around radiotherapy marks, suggest that he has developed radiation oesophagitis, a common complication of radiotherapy. As a result, his oral intake has decreased considerably, ending in multiple electrolytes abnormalities. In view of the long QTc, it is a priority to replace magnesium first in this case.

Naso-gastric tube insertion and artificial feeding
This patient has recently received radiotherapy for lung cancer and has probably developed radiation oesophagitis. The insertion of a naso-gastric tube may be appropriate as a subsequent measure to ensure caloric intake and appropriate nutrients are provided; however, in view of the long QTc, IV magnesium replacement is the next most appropriate intervention.
